$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y)}-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z & =x+K \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡z & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y)=C-2x\,\,
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5c6152f7-42f5-56fc-b75a-263cd69c9d19"] :db/ensure "q-149723" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+2}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=\frac{x+C}{x+y},
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int (\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2 & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{z} \\ {v}^{′}=1 & \,⟹\,v=z\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)-\int \text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)-z & =x+C \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1) & =x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1) & =x+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1 & =\frac{x+C}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-25217a67-7d84-5b06-8801-01edf4363fd0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-25217a67-7d84-5b06-8801-01edf4363fd0" :answer-field/id #uuid "25217a67-7d84-5b06-8801-01edf4363fd0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d60567b6-30a5-5299-bff7-543ccd03c29b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-807b691f-3c19-516b-a689-d6024d5b6077" "answer-f6059557-3dac-50d0-8066-8dd8cc82e79c" "answer-2e716eff-4358-55b4-8561-ca1c8320c525" "answer-d60567b6-30a5-5299-bff7-543ccd03c29b" "answer-47901134-19b2-5653-9a75-9c013a497690"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-807b691f-3c19-516b-a689-d6024d5b6077" :answer/id #uuid "807b691f-3c19-516b-a689-d6024d5b6077" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f6059557-3dac-50d0-8066-8dd8cc82e79c" :answer/id #uuid "f6059557-3dac-50d0-8066-8dd8cc82e79c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2e716eff-4358-55b4-8561-ca1c8320c525" :answer/id #uuid "2e716eff-4358-55b4-8561-ca1c8320c525" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d60567b6-30a5-5299-bff7-543ccd03c29b" :answer/id #uuid "d60567b6-30a5-5299-bff7-543ccd03c29b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-47901134-19b2-5653-9a75-9c013a497690" :answer/id #uuid "47901134-19b2-5653-9a75-9c013a497690" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168103 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a differential equation of the form 

$$
y ' = f ( a x + b y ),
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are real constants. In this case, we can rewrite the equation as a separable differential equation using the substitution $z= ax+by.$ We then proceed to solve this separable equation.

 To see how we apply this method, let's consider the following example: 

$$
y' = (x+y)^2
$$

First, we make the substitution

$$
z = x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 1 + \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} - 1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = g(z)$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = z^2+ 1.
$$

Notice that this differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡z & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the general solution to the equation in terms of $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\arctan {(x+y)}  = x + C
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166982 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124442 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a8c3fd0e-01dd-58d7-b5d0-e6ecb2b5f479"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-a8c3fd0e-01dd-58d7-b5d0-e6ecb2b5f479" :question/id #uuid "a8c3fd0e-01dd-58d7-b5d0-e6ecb2b5f479" :question/math-academy-id "q-65054" :question/problem "Evaluate ${f}_{zyx}(1,1,-1)$ for $f(x,y,z)=xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{z}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =xy\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =\frac{xy}{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{zy}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zy}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{z}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{xy}{x+y+z}) \\  & =\frac{x\cdot (x+y+z)-xy\cdot (1)}{(x+y+z)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+xy+xz-xy}{(x+y+z)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+xz}{(x+y+z)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{zyx}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{zy}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zy}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}+xz}{(x+y+z)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{(2x+z)\cdot (x+y+z)^{2}-({x}^{2}+xz)\cdot (2(x+y+z)\cdot 1)}{(x+y+z)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{(2x+z)(x+y+z)-2({x}^{2}+xz)}{(x+y+z)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{zyx}(x,y,z)$ at $(1,1,-1):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyx}(1,1,-1) & =\frac{(2(1)+(-1))(1+1+(-1))-2({1}^{2}+1(-1))}{(1+1+(-1))^{3}}=\frac{(1)(1)-2(0)}{(1)^{3}}=1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-58cd874b-d401-5dae-a003-642f47b6d5e1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192795 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e74f917e-f8d4-558a-b0ff-23f924d4f647"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192982 :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼B(5,\theta )$ with unknown probability of success $\theta .$ You're given the particular sample 

$$
{x}_{1}=5,\,{x}_{2}=3,\,{x}_{3}=2,\,{x}_{4}=1.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡a+b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +c\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=5$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{5-x},\,x=0,1,…,5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

:question/worked-solution "We distribute both terms of the binomial to the trinomial in the second parenthesis. $$
\eqalign{
		(x - 3)(x^2 - 2x + 6) &= \
		x(x^2 - 2x + 6) - 3(x^2 - 2x + 6) &= \
		x^3 - 2x^2 + 6x - 3x^2 + 6x - 18 &= \
		x^3 - 5x^2 + 12x - 18
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064277 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d7c22bb7-72a0-576c-8d37-5df7a0b2d33e" "question-efb60196-718e-5a66-900b-f5c4e1c9517a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064120 :question/problem "Given that  $(3s^2 + 2s - 1)(s^2 + s + 2) = 3s^4 + \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{a}s^3 + \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{b}s^2 + \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{c}s - 2,$ calculate $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify.

$$
\begin{aligned}(3{s}^{2}+2s-1)({s}^{2}+s+2) & = \\ 3{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+s+2)+2s({s}^{2}+s+2)+(-1)({s}^{2}+s+2) & = \\ 3{s}^{4}+3{s}^{3}+6{s}^{2}+2{s}^{3}+2{s}^{2}+4s-{s}^{2}-s-2 & = \\ 3{s}^{4}+5{s}^{3}+7{s}^{2}+3s-2\end{aligned}
$$

Matching up the coefficients, we find that $a=5,$ $b=7,$ and $c=3.$

So, we have

$$
a + b + c = 5 + 7 + 3 = 15.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064278 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ad1d70aa-42cb-5c9b-8e55-ba51dafe3613" "question-6568de84-d0cb-5425-90cd-1a3ef070df84"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064121 :question/problem "What is the coefficient of $a^2b$ in the product $(a+b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)?$" :question/worked-solution "We distribute both terms of the binomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify by collecting like terms.

For example, to multiply $({\color{blue}{x}} + {\color{red}{3}})$ and $(x^2 + 2x+4),$ we multiply ${\color{blue}{x}}$ and $(x^2 + 2x+4),$ and then we add this to the product of ${\color{red}{3}}$ and $(x^2 + 2x+4).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)({x}^{2}+2x+4) & = \\ x({x}^{2}+2x+4)+3({x}^{2}+2x+4) & = \\ {x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+4x+3{x}^{2}+6x+12\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we group the like terms and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+4x+3{x}^{2}+6x+12 & = \\ {x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+3{x}^{2}+4x+6x+12 & = \\ {x}^{3}+5{x}^{2}+10x+12\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064448 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186304363 :answer-field/choices 17592186302775] [:db/retract 17592186304119 :answer-field/choices 17592186302805] [:db/retract 17592186304734 :answer-field/choices 17592186303265] [:db/retract 17592186311172 :answer-field/choices 17592186310756] [:db/retract 17592186311223 :answer-field/choices 17592186310735] [:db/retract 17592186311278 :answer-field/choices 17592186308941] [:db/retract 17592186167185 :question/answer-fields 17592186164135] [:db/retract 17592186167185 :question/answer-fields 17592186164136] {:db/id 17592186166936 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2f885aae-2228-5978-9940-05380822e48d" "question-dc370c50-c95d-53af-9285-c137ac273145"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166524 :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
![](images/31/3139ce9adc8c4803bc8cf3332e76c2bad4cb35489024478178ab74023dee7e44.svg)

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-2{e}^{-4t})-2{e}^{-4t}\cdot {e}^{3t}}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{3t} & -2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{t} \\ -\frac{17}{10}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{17}{10}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166938 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-858d57fe-416e-56c5-af8b-4ea6e4298062"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166526 :question/problem "![](images/2a/2a4a67e816a9de4c0278f607d2e98ceae6cbd315df086980d7a604da88ed1926.svg)

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}_c(t) + \mathbf{x}_p(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_c(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that
![](images/85/8570eb051b14077d86cbe0cda29f79d12de8529001c6e9b3a2698c107792ef1b.svg)

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
![](images/9f/9fe602a563fbfbfd3f3331df7243ebf1aa5aa1c90a01550a033d4a4dfd0f0639.svg)

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-4t}-0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 0\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=2t$ and $\text{d}v=e^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{2t}-\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, the integrand is zero, so the integral is zero.

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2t-1) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2t-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186304363 :answer-field/correct 17592186303295 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186304119 :answer-field/correct 17592186303429 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186304734 :answer-field/correct 17592186303782 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186311172 :answer-field/correct 17592186308746 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186311223 :answer-field/correct 17592186309507 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186311278 :answer-field/correct 17592186310337 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-2f885aae-2228-5978-9940-05380822e48d" :question/id #uuid "2f885aae-2228-5978-9940-05380822e48d" :question/math-academy-id "q-336714" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-4}} both sides of the equation." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}\text{ and }\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}

:question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-2}} by substitution.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-3}} ." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields <td height="30px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" height="40px" rowspan="2"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td height="60px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center">$\frac{4}{3}{e}^{-t}$</td>
<td align="center"></td>
<td height="60px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center">$\frac{9}{5}$</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{-4t} & -{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}4{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-{e}^{2t})-3{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{-4t}}[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{2t} \\ -{e}^{-4t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2t}}{3}[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{2t} \\ -{e}^{-4t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{4t} \\ \frac{1}{3}{e}^{-2t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{4t} \\ \frac{1}{3}{e}^{-2t} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{3}{e}^{5t} \\ \frac{4}{3}{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$

$$

$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}6t \\ 3t\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot 3{e}^{-2t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6t \\ 3t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3t{e}^{2t} \\ 12t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-3t{e}^{2t} \\ 12t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -3t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 12t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-3\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$

- For the second component, let $u=12t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=12\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =12t\cdot {e}^{t}-\int 12\cdot {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =12t{e}^{t}-12{e}^{t} \\  & =12{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(4t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =4t{e}^{t}-4{e}^{t} \\  & =4{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ -\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}36(t-1)-(3t+1) \\ -(3t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}33t-37 \\ -3t-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9324a6eb-07ab-5ed4-84d0-646338f3a965"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9324a6eb-07ab-5ed4-84d0-646338f3a965" :answer-field/id #uuid "9324a6eb-07ab-5ed4-84d0-646338f3a965" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-a8039f17-10a2-5a2d-8787-b1e6d3df2d80" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a8039f17-10a2-5a2d-8787-b1e6d3df2d80"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a8039f17-10a2-5a2d-8787-b1e6d3df2d80" :answer/id #uuid "a8039f17-10a2-5a2d-8787-b1e6d3df2d80" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "33t-37" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167991 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of ordinary differential equations

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) =
A
\mathbf{x}(t) +
\mathbf{f}(t)
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix and $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is a forcing vector.

In this lesson, we'll derive the formula for the particular solution of the above system using the method of variation of parameters.

Recall that the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_c(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{c}$ is a vector of constants, and $\Phi$ is the fundamental matrix.

As usual, for the method of variation of parameters, we'll look for a particular solution of our inhomogeneous system by varying the constant parameters, i.e., in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined.

Differentiating $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φ\,u(t))^{′} \\  & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a solution, substituting it back into the initial system gives a true equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, $\Phi' = A \Phi.$ Substituting this into the equation simplifies it to the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+AΦu(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t) & =f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $\Phi$ is invertible, we can pre-multiply both sides by $\Phi^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate both sides of the final equations (ignoring the constant term):

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \displaystyle\int \Phi^{-1}\mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166985 :activity/expected-seconds 1500.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186061086 :answer-field/choices 17592186061088] [:db/retract 17592186061086 :answer-field/choices 17592186061089] [:db/retract 17592186061086 :answer-field/choices 17592186061090] [:db/retract 17592186061086 :answer-field/choices 17592186061091] [:db/retract 17592186061086 :answer-field/choices 17592186061087] {:db/id 17592186064247 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f8a011fe-bff7-586f-86e9-fabb797df0e3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064002 :question/problem "Factor the quadratic expression $10a^2 + 11a + 3.$" :question/worked-solution "We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
10a^2 + 11a + 3.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($10 \times 3 = 30$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($11$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $30.$

The positive factor pairs of $30$ are

$$
(1,30), \quad (2,15), \quad (3,10), \quad (5,6).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(5,6)$ add to $11{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5+6 & =11\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $5a + 6a,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}10{a}^{2}+11a+3 & = \\ 10{a}^{2}+5a+6a+3 & = \\ (10{a}^{2}+5a)+(6a+3) & = \\ 5a(2a+1)+3(2a+1) & = \\ (5a+3)(2a+1) & \end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064248 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d54b0636-ad05-55a6-91c9-9613b500f9d1" "question-433698fd-3b83-5c8a-9280-a485202f8699"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064004 :question/problem "Factor the quadratic expression $2c^2 + 15c - 8.$" :question/worked-solution "We must factor the quadratic expression

:question/math-academy-id "q-52254" :question/problem "Factor $5{h}^{2}-12h-9.$" :question/worked-solution "We must factor the quadratic expression

{{field-3}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "We must factor the quadratic expression

$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($4\times 9=36$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($-15$).

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the product of the quadratic coefficient and constant is positive, we only need to consider the negative factor pairs of $36.$

The negative factor pairs of $36$ are

$$
(-1,-36),\,(-2,-18),\,(-3,-12),\,(-4,-9),\,(-6,-6).

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-3,-12)$ add to $-15:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)+(-12) & =-15\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-3x-12x,$ and factor the result by grouping:

:answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065449 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to factor quadratic trinomials whose quadratic coefficient equals one. In this lesson, we'll extend our understanding to include cases where the quadratic coefficient is a positive integer that's different from one.

For example, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
{\color{red}{2}}x^2+{\color{purple}{7}}x+{\color{blue}{3}}
$$

 

Notice that the quadratic coefficient equals ${\color{red}{2}}.$

To factor this trinomial, we must find two numbers that 

- *multiply* to give the *product* of the quadratic coefficient and the constant $({\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{blue}{3}} = 6),$ and

- *add* to give the linear coefficient $({\color{purple}{7}})$.

We can factor this trinomial in four steps:

- **Step 1:**  We start by writing down the factor pairs of $6{:}$

The factor pairs of $6$ are

$$
(1,6), \qquad (2,3).
$$

- **Step 2:**  Determine which of these factor pairs add up to the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{7}})\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+6 & =7 & ✓ \\ 2+3 & =5 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 3:**  Using the factor pair identified in the previous step, write the linear term as $7x=x+6x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+7x+3 & = \\ 2{x}^{2}+x+6x+3\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 4:**  Factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+x+6x+3 & = \\ x(2x+1)+3(2x+1) & = \\ (2x+1)(x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

And we're done! 

We can check that our answer is correct by expanding the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x+1)(x+3) & = \\ 2x\cdot (x+3)+1\cdot (x+3) & = \\ 2{x}^{2}+6x+x+3 & = \\ 2{x}^{2}+7x+3 & \,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065450 :tutorial/content "To factor a quadratic expression, we must find a factor pair of the *product* of the quadratic coefficient and the constant that adds to the linear coefficient.

With that in mind, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
{\color{red}{2}}y^2 {\color{purple}{\,-\,7}}y + {\color{blue}{3}}
$$

Notice that,

- the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant, ${\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{blue}{3}} = 6$, is *positive*, while

- the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}})$ is *negative*.

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the product of the quadratic coefficient and constant is positive, we need to consider the *negative* factor pairs of $6.$

The negative factor pairs of $6$ are

$$
(-1,-6), \quad (-2,-3).
$$

For each pair, their *product* is positive, and their sum is *negative*, which is what we want.

Now, we determine which of these factor pairs sums to the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}}){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)+(-6) & =-7\,✓ \\ (-2)+(-3) & =-5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-y - 6y,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-7y+3 & = \\ 2{y}^{2}-y-6y+3 & = \\ (2{y}^{2}-y)-(6y-3) & = \\ y(2y-1)-3(2y-1) & = \\ (y-3)(2y-1) & \end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064458 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "activity-573c8163-64a6-518f-9257-259186333e47" :activity/id #uuid "adc246a5-558f-5836-8eea-ace518963371" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168064 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to write the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf v\in \mathbb R^n$ relative some general basis $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^n.$ In this lesson, we will generalize this concept to abstract vector spaces.

As an example, consider the matrices $A_1$ and $A_2,$ given by

![](images/28/2828c037a750f078b4d98b93248e800ec05d4899d7eb390dd135326314c44e70.svg)

The set $\mathcal{B}=\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ is a basis of the vector space $V = \textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}.$ Now, suppose that the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ are 

![](images/2d/2db3ab1e4452eff2f19151cc87a805452433c7f305a80e5480c25241cba42c38.svg)

Let's find the matrix $C$ using this information. 

As usual, any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
x_1 A_1  + x_2 A_2,
$$

where $x_1,x_2$ are the coordinates of the vector relative to the basis. 

In our case, we have 

![](images/64/6489e130a9237881664e1649cc5408cdff87cfb12dcf44c0342b9961cdf7bc81.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]+4\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 12 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 10 \\ 8 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168065 :tutorial/content "Suppose we fix a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with scalars from $\mathbb{R}$ (note that "finite-dimensional" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element $\mathbf{v} \in V$ using the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}$

![](images/c9/c9297a30f87baf08295a752cb23f2d314139508f875b4ffa2fffc8763656bd54.svg)

This defines a bijective mapping $\phi: V\to \mathbb{R}^n.$ Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:

- $\phi(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = \phi(\mathbf{u}) + \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V,$ and

- $\phi(\alpha \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}.$

Because of this, we say that $V$ is **isomorphic** to $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Intuitively, this means that $V$ and $\mathbb R^n$ have identical structures.

to evaluate the expression $\sqrt x + 3$ for the value $x=9.$ This type of expression is called a **radical expression** because it contains the radical symbol $\sqrt{\phantom 0}.$ Remember that $\sqrt x$ means "the positive square root of the number $x.$" 

To evaluate this expression at the given value, we replace $x$ with $9$ in the given expression and simplify.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x}+3 & = \\ \sqrt{9}+3 & = \\ \sqrt{{3}^{2}}+3 & = \\ 3+3 & = \\ 6\end{aligned}
$$

**Important:** You may have heard somewhere that $\sqrt{9} = \pm 3,$ because $(-3)^2=9$ and $(3)^2 = 9.$ However, when we write down $\sqrt{9},$ we *always* mean "the positive square root of $9$".

If we want the negative square root of $9$, we write $-\sqrt{9} = -3.$ Sometimes, we want both, in which case we would write $\pm\sqrt{9}=\pm 3.$"] [17592186134037 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-4126f1c5-7567-585d-9e49-d37c72e8e18c" :question/id #uuid "4126f1c5-7567-585d-9e49-d37c72e8e18c"] ["question-4126f1c5-7567-585d-9e49-d37c72e8e18c" :question/math-academy-id "q-162753"] ["question-4126f1c5-7567-585d-9e49-d37c72e8e18c" :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)=4x-2y+1\,$ on the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=5.$"] ["question-4126f1c5-7567-585d-9e49-d37c72e8e18c" :question/worked-solution "We must find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=5.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=5
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4,-2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}4=2\lambda x \\ -2=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{2}{\lambda } \\ y=-\frac{1}{\lambda }\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=5$ and solve for $\lambda ,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =5 \\ \frac{4}{{\lambda }^{2}}+\frac{1}{{\lambda }^{2}} & =5 \\ \frac{5}{{\lambda }^{2}} & =5 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =1 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $x$ and $y.$ This gives

$$
x=\pm 2,\,y=∓1.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-2,1),\,(2,-1).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $\,(x,y)\,$ | $(-2,1)$ | $(2,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-9$ | $11$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-2,1),$ and its minimum value is $-9.$"] ["question-4126f1c5-7567-585d-9e49-d37c72e8e18c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$

$$

$$

$$

(0,-2),\,(\pm \sqrt{2},-1).

\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{5}{1-5x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-25(1-5x)^{-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=0.$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(0)=-\frac{25}{(1-5\cdot 0)^{2}}=-25.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of ${x}^{2},$ as follows:

$$

["question-80893bd5-f8f9-5d69-b7d0-36e40ddfd184" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$"] ["question-80893bd5-f8f9-5d69-b7d0-36e40ddfd184" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-80893bd5-f8f9-5d69-b7d0-36e40ddfd184" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-63f7e3dc-e6fb-53cc-b486-dbf54e61e1b3" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{y}^{′}+5y=3{e}^{-5x},
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-5x}$, find the particular solution to the equation.

${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-178b0d68-b124-5a5b-940e-16d447e5211f" :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

We see that the right-hand side is $3{e}^{-5x},$ and ${e}^{-5x}$ is a term in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-5x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

We calculate the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ using the product rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha x{e}^{-5x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{-5x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{-5x}-5x{e}^{-5x}) \\  & =\alpha (1-5x){e}^{-5x}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\alpha (1-5x){e}^{-5x})+5\alpha x{e}^{-5x} & =3{e}^{-5x} \\ (1-5x+5x)\alpha {e}^{-5x} & =3{e}^{-5x} \\ \alpha {e}^{-5x} & =3{e}^{-5x} \\ \alpha  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3x{e}^{-5x}.
$$"] ["question-178b0d68-b124-5a5b-940e-16d447e5211f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-9a4120a4-2ac8-5351-bb5f-79cfef062572" :answer-field/id #uuid "9a4120a4-2ac8-5351-bb5f-79cfef062572"] ["answer-5e163fd4-f82d-598e-bb46-e9eb87f8d20c" :answer/id #uuid "5e163fd4-f82d-598e-bb46-e9eb87f8d20c"] ["answer-5e163fd4-f82d-598e-bb46-e9eb87f8d20c" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-5e163fd4-f82d-598e-bb46-e9eb87f8d20c" :answer/value "3xe^{-5x}"] ["answer-field-9a4120a4-2ac8-5351-bb5f-79cfef062572" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-9a4120a4-2ac8-5351-bb5f-79cfef062572" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-9a4120a4-2ac8-5351-bb5f-79cfef062572" :answer-field/correct "answer-5e163fd4-f82d-598e-bb46-e9eb87f8d20c"] ["answer-field-9a4120a4-2ac8-5351-bb5f-79cfef062572" :answer-field/choices "answer-5e163fd4-f82d-598e-bb46-e9eb87f8d20c"] ["question-178b0d68-b124-5a5b-940e-16d447e5211f" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-9a4120a4-2ac8-5351-bb5f-79cfef062572"] [17592186229163 :knowledge-point/questions "question-178b0d68-b124-5a5b-940e-16d447e5211f"] ["question-5c8f03a1-964a-5fd4-a60f-a2aa229186e2" :question/id #uuid "5c8f03a1-964a-5fd4-a60f-a2aa229186e2"] ["question-5c8f03a1-964a-5fd4-a60f-a2aa229186e2" :question/math-academy-id "q-43048"] ["question-5c8f03a1-964a-5fd4-a60f-a2aa229186e2" :question/problem "Consider the matrices given below. Given that $A$ and $B$ are row equivalent matrices and $det(A)=6$, find $det(B).$

$$"] ["question-5c8f03a1-964a-5fd4-a60f-a2aa229186e2" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $B$ can be obtained from $A$ by swapping the $2$nd and the $3$rd rows.

$f(x,y,z)=z-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3,$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$"] ["question-d215478d-b523-59e2-bf03-ca21eb9b301e" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=3.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ z-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3 & =3 \\ z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=3$ is the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$"] ["question-d215478d-b523-59e2-bf03-ca21eb9b301e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "step-fedc8bb3-4406-5d39-8711-ea07b719c253"] [17592186138186 :question/problem "Expand $(x + 3)(x - 3).$"] [17592186138186 :question/worked-solution "We will use the difference of square formula:

$$
(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2
$$

Substituting $a=x$ and $b=3,$ we have

$$
\eqalign{
		(x + 3)(x - 3) &= \[5pt]
		x^2 - 3^2 &= \[5pt]
		x^2 - 9.
	}
$$"] [17592186138187 :question/problem "Expand $(5x - 4)(5x + 4) .$"] [17592186138187 :question/worked-solution "We will use the difference of square formula:

$$
(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2
$$

Substituting $a=5x$ and $b=4,$ we have

$$
\eqalign{
		(5x - 4)(5x + 4) &= \[5pt]
		(5x)^2 - (4)^2 &= \[5pt]
		25x^2 - 16.
	}
$$"] [17592186138188 :question/problem "Expand $(6x + y^2)(6x - y^2) .$"] [17592186138188 :question/worked-solution "We will use the difference of square formula:

$$
(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2
$$

Substituting $a=6x$ and $b=y^2,$ we have

$$
\eqalign{
		(6x + y^2)(6x - y^2) &= \[5pt]
		(6x)^2 - \left(y^2\right)^2 &= \[5pt]
		36x^2 - y^4.
	}
$$"] [17592186138189 :question/problem "Expand $(2x^n-1)(2x^n+1).$"] [17592186138189 :question/worked-solution "We will use the difference of square formula:

$$
(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2
$$

Substituting $a=2x^n$ and $b=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{x}^{n}-1)(2{x}^{n}+1) & = \\ {(2{x}^{n})}^{2}-(1)^{2} & = \\ {2}^{2}\cdot ({x}^{n})^{2}-1 & = \\ 4{x}^{2n}-1.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6c871005-09ff-5497-b5c8-d9bfa75173ab" :question/id #uuid "6c871005-09ff-5497-b5c8-d9bfa75173ab"] ["question-6c871005-09ff-5497-b5c8-d9bfa75173ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-110716"] ["question-6c871005-09ff-5497-b5c8-d9bfa75173ab" :question/problem "$(9-y)(9+y)=$"] ["question-6c871005-09ff-5497-b5c8-d9bfa75173ab" :question/worked-solution "We will use the difference of squares formula:

:answer-field/choices "answer-b3e00615-af87-5a34-8ad3-47a40357e4de"] [17592186137860 :answer-field/choices "answer-754ba023-6388-50a6-b77b-a9be36a73709"] [17592186139725 :tutorial/content "The **difference of squares formula** states the product of the sum and the difference of two monomials is equal to the difference of their squares:

$$
(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2
$$

We can check that this result is correct by expanding the binomial in the usual way, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		({\color{blue}a} + {\color{red}b})(a - b) &= \[5pt]
		{\color{blue}a}(a - b) + {\color{red}b}(a - b) &= \[5pt]
		a^2 - ab + ab - b^2 &= \[5pt]
		a^2 - b^2 \,& {\color{green}{\checkmark}}
	}
$$

Notice that the middle two terms $- ab$ and $ab$ cancel each other out, leaving only $a^2 - b^2.$ 

If the order of multiplication is switched, the formula still remains the same:

$$
(a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2
$$"] [17592186138601 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-888487e0-300d-510a-97fe-31196306b818" :question/id #uuid "888487e0-300d-510a-97fe-31196306b818"] ["question-888487e0-300d-510a-97fe-31196306b818" :question/math-academy-id "q-81344"] ["question-888487e0-300d-510a-97fe-31196306b818" :question/problem "If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the curves $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and $y=x-1,$ then ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA=$"] ["question-888487e0-300d-510a-97fe-31196306b818" :question/worked-solution "First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/24/24683f81da1c7e90ccbd51748f5f46407137be4a40ef5f0678292b70f0781eff.png)

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2} & =x-1 \\ {x}^{2}+x-2 & =0 \\ (x+2)(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$-2\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/e9/e955ad94bca70a8e6f996d81814ffa8fcc7a322d5979db7b0726d39558b6aa86.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 1,\,x-1\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{x-1}^{1-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{x-1}^{1-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-888487e0-300d-510a-97fe-31196306b818" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-6b82a6ed-9537-5fe1-9550-c6deec72fd33" :answer-field/id #uuid where $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and below the $x$-axis."] ["question-c45bffe5-25bf-5869-8e87-fa24cb3ec218" :question/worked-solution "Since $y\le 0,$ we obtain

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1\,⟹\,y=-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}.

Let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/9c/9c6b1dd7d81d124888ddd588027eed908a0eaecb2c42ebc79f3253c4123dbe86.png)

- We already know the intersection of the circle with the line $y=0.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$-1\le x\le 1.$

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\le y\le 0\}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}8x{y}^{3}\,dA={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}8x{y}^{3}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}8x{y}^{3}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x[{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}4{y}^{3}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x{[{y}^{4}]}_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x(0-{(-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}})}^{4})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2x(1-{x}^{2})^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2x(1-{x}^{2})^{2})\,dx & ={[\frac{(1-{x}^{2})^{3}}{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{(1-{1}^{2})^{3}}{3}-\frac{(1-(-1)^{2})^{3}}{3} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c45bffe5-25bf-5869-8e87-fa24cb3ec218" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-6d527e9c-2e5b-5948-a599-77a3b28decc4" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{7\pi }{6},$ shown above?"] ["question-49e7f17d-b251-56fb-a73b-9aa663a5feb5" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{(1-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{1-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +25{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +25{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{1-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +25}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{26-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-49e7f17d-b251-56fb-a73b-9aa663a5feb5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-86b07591-e098-5b5d-80e3-d30542d3cd68" :answer-field/id #uuid Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above."] ["question-6017b841-30bb-5249-81e7-cac41367e88a" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =8(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6017b841-30bb-5249-81e7-cac41367e88a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-416c49b7-a3b7-5531-9507-24f1c4541b91" :answer-field/id #uuid Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?"] ["question-e4160743-42ed-5b1d-80ee-6f99ed405134" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

["question-22b679e5-bd2f-5f85-b6e8-97dc0feb70a5" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\theta {e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=(1+\theta ){e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\theta {e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{((1+\theta ){e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}{e}^{2\theta }+(1+\theta )^{2}{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{e}^{2\theta }({\theta }^{2}+1+2\theta +{\theta }^{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{\theta }\sqrt{2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-22b679e5-bd2f-5f85-b6e8-97dc0feb70a5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a8b124e2-32da-5651-8541-39b8419c32ee" :answer-field/id #uuid Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2},$ shown above."] ["question-dcd1fd46-503a-5471-9362-496d88e411cc" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}).
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{({cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}))}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{6}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})[{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})]}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}[1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\theta }{3})]\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\theta +\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\theta }{3})]}_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dcd1fd46-503a-5471-9362-496d88e411cc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-87114391-cb4d-5092-83cc-b2e18baed326" :answer-field/id #uuid "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}yz)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})) \\  & =2xyz+{x}^{3}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-1,-1,2),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F(-1,-1,2) & =2(-1)(-1)(2)+(-1)^{3}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-1}{-1}) \\  & =4-1+\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =3+\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-75ca7d55-6e3f-58c8-8a50-805ce5d1a756" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-346d1a8e-e297-5ff1-8dff-7d5740531d20" :answer-field/id #uuid "![](images/2b/2b64c156519b685acf390c51c1ea3e1540d82e0f7e047cf2f804d38a23956604.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

I. $∇\cdot F=0$

II. $∇\cdot F>0$

III. $∇\cdot F<0$

IV. $F$ is solenoidal"] ["question-3aad6c37-ff96-5a6c-89b9-a9f32a30b3d7" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement II is true, whereas statements I and III are false. Notice that the length of the vectors' $x$-components increase as we move away from the origin in the horizontal direction. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a source at every point.

- Statement IV is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""] ["question-3aad6c37-ff96-5a6c-89b9-a9f32a30b3d7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-22420a9a-1575-5698-aa34-04729efa2a61" hectares."] ["question-319f568f-1d7f-56e6-aaee-eed8bdcd4507" :question/worked-solution "The exact area of land is ${(\frac{7}{9})}^{2}$ hectares.

Writing ${(\frac{7}{9})}^{2}$ with multiplication signs, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{7}{9})}^{2} & ={{\frac{7}{9}\times \frac{7}{9}}_{⏟}}_{2\text{ times}} \\  & =\frac{7\times 7}{9\times 9} \\  & =\frac{49}{81}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$\,$liters of liquid fertilizer left over."] ["question-e29d8681-5a80-5808-b535-ab9dc2e4503c" :question/worked-solution "Orlando had $(10\,\frac{1}{2}-9\,\frac{1}{6})$ liters of liquid fertilizer left over.

Writing $10\,\frac{1}{2}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
10\,\frac{1}{2}=\frac{10\times 2+1}{2}=\frac{21}{2}.
$$

Writing $9\,\frac{1}{6}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
9\,\frac{1}{6}=\frac{9\times 6+1}{6}=\frac{55}{6}.
$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{21}{2}-\frac{55}{6}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $6.$

To put $\frac{21}{2}$ over a denominator of $6,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $3:$

$$
\frac{21}{2}=\frac{21\times 3}{2\times 3}=\frac{63}{6}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators:

$$
\frac{63}{6}-\frac{55}{6}=\frac{8}{6}
$$

Simplifying, we have

$$
\frac{8}{6}=\frac{8÷2}{6÷2}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
\frac{4}{3}=1\,\text{R}\,1=1\,\frac{1}{3}
$$

Therefore, Orlando had $1\,\frac{1}{3}$ liters of liquid fertilizer left over."] ["question-e29d8681-5a80-5808-b535-ab9dc2e4503c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-5138ec1b-11c8-5624-8ae0-30b14a7ff9f7" :answer-field/id #uuid "5138ec1b-11c8-5624-8ae0-30b14a7ff9f7"] ["answer-a23b3b85-3b3f-5cad-b5eb-d6d6c2bf5943" :answer/id #uuid "a23b3b85-3b3f-5cad-b5eb-d6d6c2bf5943"] ["answer-a23b3b85-3b3f-5cad-b5eb-d6d6c2bf5943" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-a23b3b85-3b3f-5cad-b5eb-d6d6c2bf5943" :answer/value "1\,\frac{1}{3}"] ["answer-field-5138ec1b-11c8-5624-8ae0-30b14a7ff9f7" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-5138ec1b-11c8-5624-8ae0-30b14a7ff9f7" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-5138ec1b-11c8-5624-8ae0-30b14a7ff9f7" :answer-field/correct "answer-a23b3b85-3b3f-5cad-b5eb-d6d6c2bf5943"] ["answer-field-5138ec1b-11c8-5624-8ae0-30b14a7ff9f7" :answer-field/choices "answer-a23b3b85-3b3f-5cad-b5eb-d6d6c2bf5943"] ["question-e29d8681-5a80-5808-b535-ab9dc2e4503c" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-5138ec1b-11c8-5624-8ae0-30b14a7ff9f7"] [17592186073705 :knowledge-point/questions "question-e29d8681-5a80-5808-b535-ab9dc2e4503c"] ["question-5606b628-dd5a-51e3-a0c0-f4f6b8db27d7" :question/id #uuid "5606b628-dd5a-51e3-a0c0-f4f6b8db27d7"] ["question-5606b628-dd5a-51e3-a0c0-f4f6b8db27d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-166809"] ["question-5606b628-dd5a-51e3-a0c0-f4f6b8db27d7" :question/problem "Orlando bought $6$ packages of powdered fertilizer, for which he paid $$96.44.$ Estimate the price of each package by rounding the amount of money he spent to the nearest dollar.

\begin{aligned}3-{y}^{3} & ={y}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{3} & =3 \\ {y}^{3} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}

So, $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

$$

:question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type II region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,2{y}^{2}\le x\le {y}^{2}+1\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}y\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}y\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[\,x\,]_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y({y}^{2}+1-2{y}^{2})dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["activity-deb6a015-5188-5c6d-9bbf-340e569612da" :activity/id #uuid "deb6a015-5188-5c6d-9bbf-340e569612da"] ["step-b77fee23-8b22-50d7-96e8-1c58b86a3b31" :step/id #uuid - Parentheses $()$ to indicate that the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ to indicate that the endpoints *are* included.

$$
[-1,2\,)

$$
-1\,\,\le \,\,y\,\,<\,\,2.
$$"] ["question-8242dd7c-9e76-5a08-b5a0-1fe98445b603" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d78e9d72-459d-5fce-90e1-8180676b9ebb" :answer-field/id #uuid "Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{{e}^{y-x}}{x-y+1}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$"] ["question-0ebc5c12-2f6e-589d-af5a-42a020eb709e" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-\frac{{e}^{-z}}{z+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{-z}}{z+1}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+1){e}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int (z+1){e}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z+1 & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{z} & \,⟹\,v={e}^{z}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (z+1){e}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ (z+1){e}^{z}-\int {e}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ (z+1){e}^{z}-{e}^{z} & =x+C \\ z{e}^{z} & =x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
(x-y){e}^{x-y}=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=(x-y){e}^{x-y}.$"] ["question-0ebc5c12-2f6e-589d-af5a-42a020eb709e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-0d6cf9d9-7b5d-5a12-954e-3a9a145111eb" "question-0ebc5c12-2f6e-589d-af5a-42a020eb709e"] ["question-943c59c7-5044-5ab4-92f0-26722bf35b20" :question/id #uuid "943c59c7-5044-5ab4-92f0-26722bf35b20"] ["question-943c59c7-5044-5ab4-92f0-26722bf35b20" :question/math-academy-id "q-108838"] ["question-943c59c7-5044-5ab4-92f0-26722bf35b20" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y)}-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$"] ["question-943c59c7-5044-5ab4-92f0-26722bf35b20" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z & =x+K \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡z & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y)=C-2x\,\,
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y).$"] ["question-943c59c7-5044-5ab4-92f0-26722bf35b20" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] "question-943c59c7-5044-5ab4-92f0-26722bf35b20"] ["question-1808d5b9-dae6-5dea-b5bd-62c618289147" :question/id #uuid "1808d5b9-dae6-5dea-b5bd-62c618289147"] ["question-1808d5b9-dae6-5dea-b5bd-62c618289147" :question/math-academy-id "q-149723"] ["question-1808d5b9-dae6-5dea-b5bd-62c618289147" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+2}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=\frac{x+C}{x+y},
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$"] ["question-1808d5b9-dae6-5dea-b5bd-62c618289147" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int (\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2 & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{z} \\ {v}^{′}=1 & \,⟹\,v=z\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)-\int \text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)-z & =x+C \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1) & =x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1) & =x+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1 & =\frac{x+C}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1.$"] ["question-1808d5b9-dae6-5dea-b5bd-62c618289147" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-25217a67-7d84-5b06-8801-01edf4363fd0"
