- The operation ${R}_{6}:={R}_{6}+(-7){R}_{2}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{1}:=\frac{3}{4}{R}_{1}$ involves multiplying a row by $\frac{3}{4},$ so the determinant is multiplied by $\frac{3}{4}$ as well.

Therefore, we only have to multiply the determinant by $\frac{3}{4}.$ Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Y) & =\frac{3}{4}det(X) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot 28 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5a731d48-68b1-58c7-b15e-4a787d1f4b44" :step/next {:db/id 17592186424903}} {:db/id 17592186424902 :step/content {:db/id 17592186329661 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "038f903c-07cf-5804-8ccf-c48c4437fe4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186326971} {:answer/id #uuid "5e5d0fbb-4c6d-516a-bbe1-bc9a4754768c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-20" :db/id 17592186327766} {:answer/id #uuid "7edb508d-7daa-5a42-80ea-172f811c7a6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186328025} {:answer/id #uuid "cef987a3-28b5-50d6-be17-23ad82b7d421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-15" :db/id 17592186328755} {:answer/id #uuid "dce0ee78-0312-5fae-84a0-aea62c27e409" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186328863}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186328755} :answer-field/id #uuid "91964048-e6f4-5262-9e11-ecd0686eeeaf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186329428}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "44ea0623-3f8f-525c-8344-8d911fbef23b" :question/math-academy-id "q-42504" :question/problem "Suppose $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(A)=5.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}$ and ${R}_{3}:=3{R}_{3}.$ What is the value of $det(B)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:=3{R}_{3}$ involves multiplying a row by $3,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $3$ as well.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by $3$ as well. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =3\cdot (-det(A)) \\  & =-3det(A) \\  & =-3\cdot 5 \\  & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5b098fcf-c1b8-5f75-8b3a-28dc83ab8997" :step/next {:db/id 17592186424904}} {:db/id 17592186424903 :step/content {:db/id 17592186424899 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "171230a8-065f-5312-91ff-166c6fb3df4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}" :db/id 17592186424893} {:answer/id #uuid "21bc26a0-57ad-5e62-a6e6-621e2ba24583" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}" :db/id 17592186424894} {:answer/id #uuid "54d72f80-7a7b-5b93-a0ec-2d6edad08ac4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186424895} {:answer/id #uuid "6c11e90f-184e-57bd-b3ed-1971d8fb82ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{2}:=-{R}_{2}" :db/id 17592186424896} {:answer/id #uuid "acde6755-f2db-5c6c-bdc1-ac03bdaa2931" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186424897}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424894} :answer-field/id #uuid "c75bea69-7db0-5820-97b1-b5dd95b8b845" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424898}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "200dace6-387b-586f-87ab-a5501c01cbe0" :question/math-academy-id "q-130851" :question/problem "Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 0 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}]?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}| & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 0 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "796d84ed-30ec-5eef-9c9e-3ecd61007abc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186424900}} {:db/id 17592186424904 :step/content {:db/id 17592186341855 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17922ecf-87f8-5af9-872a-3d5dc6da26af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-36" :db/id 17592186339339} {:answer/id #uuid "3e3f2587-b4ad-5bf0-81b7-1df62ffb7a09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-243" :db/id 17592186339686} {:answer/id #uuid "a21fdf0b-c950-5ec9-b67b-31a39827c266" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186340600} {:answer/id #uuid "ae1d7c41-28d1-55a3-9882-2c2b96500495" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-48" :db/id 17592186340714} {:answer/id #uuid "f3da6cbc-6c90-5ed2-9aad-88c3625d3d86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-192" :db/id 17592186341277}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341277} :answer-field/id #uuid "ded707a6-03c1-52cc-8868-8933afddd3df" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341773}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "bce6072f-0fd1-50b6-a305-a94b72b85f4e" :question/math-academy-id "q-72740" :question/problem "Suppose $Y$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $det(Y)=-3.$ What is the value of $det(4Y)?$" :question/worked-solution "Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. $$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}.

- The operation ${R}_{5}↔{R}_{6}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{2}:=\frac{4}{5}{R}_{2}$ involves multiplying a row by $\frac{4}{5},$ so the determinant is multiplied by $\frac{4}{5}$ as well.

{:activity/expected-seconds 1500.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186230044} :activity/id #uuid "e1f24137-95a9-5d07-991d-2ce3ba7ada0d" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049146 :topic/id #uuid "de6ce0f8-a513-5c11-b2ac-9d3484be570b" :topic/math-academy-id 6679} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186230044 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230177 :tutorial/content "Consider the first-order inhomogeneous ODE with constant coefficients given by

$$
ay' + by = f(x),
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

As we know, the method of finding the general solution is to find the sum of the complementary solution $y_c(x)$ and a particular solution $y_p(x).$

$$
y(x) = y_c(x) + y_p(x)
$$

To find the particular solution $y_p(x),$ we examine the functional form of the forcing term $f(x)$ and guess a form for $y_p(x)$ that matches it. 

An ODE exhibits **exponential forcing** if the forcing term $f(x)$ is an exponential function

$$
f(x) = Ke^{k x},
$$

where $K$ is a constant. 

Provided that the forcing function $e^{kx}$ is not a term in the complementary solution, our trial guess for the particular solution is an exponential function with the same exponent. That is

$$
y_p(x) = \alpha\,e^{k x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

In this lesson, we focus on solving first-order inhomogeneous ODEs with **exponential forcing**. Let's look at a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "7a60ff4f-cb9d-522a-a94a-d16f43b6a04a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14449 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0804d262-6611-5c45-bc86-10e3c26e86a2" :step/math-academy-id 597439 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230045}} {:db/id 17592186230045 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230227 :tutorial/content "Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac {\textrm{d} y} {\textrm{d} x} + 3 y = 4 e ^ {2x}.
$$

The associated homogeneous equation is

$$
\frac {\textrm{d} y} {\textrm{d} x} + 3 y = 0
$$

and therefore, the complementary solution is 

$$
y_c(x) =  A e^{-3x},
$$

 

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant. Let's now find the **particular solution** $y_p(x)$ to this equation.

Since the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is the exponential function $f(x) = 4 e^{2x},$ and this is not incorporated within the complementary solution, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(x) = \alpha e^{2x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of $y_p$ gives

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y_p}{\textrm{d}x} = 2\alpha e ^{2x}.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute $y_p$ and $y_p'$ into the differential equation and solve for $\alpha{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(2\alpha {e}^{2x})+3(\alpha {e}^{2x}) & =4{e}^{2x} \\ (2+3)\alpha {e}^{2x} & =4{e}^{2x} \\ 5\alpha {e}^{2x} & =4{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution $y_p(x)$ is

$$
y_p(x) = \dfrac{4}{5} e ^{2x}.
$$

Finally, the **general solution** is given by

$$
y = y_c + y_p = A e^{-3x} + \dfrac{4}{5} e ^{2x}.
$$

We can employ a similar strategy when the forcing function is a sum of exponential functions. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "62cac4a5-105b-5e43-8d88-63ce73a86e94" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14700 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "c3a6d6f6-44d9-519b-8417-7113691d787c" :step/math-academy-id 597440 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230046}} {:db/id 17592186230046 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229162 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228896 :question/id #uuid "5e56989a-feb1-590a-8684-9442dee1b1cb" :question/math-academy-id "e-21615"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "42bcc7e2-88f7-5ef9-8c51-77c1e2c8e8af" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049370} {:db/id 17592186050271}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229626} {:db/id 17592186229641} {:db/id 17592186305078} {:db/id 17592186305080} {:db/id 17592186305083} {:db/id 17592186305085} {:db/id 17592186305086} {:db/id 17592186305087} {:db/id 17592186305088} {:db/id 17592186305089}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Particular Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE With Exponential Forcing"} :step/id #uuid "bfa02bee-ddb6-54c2-afc0-6e67786db1f4" :step/math-academy-id 597441 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230047}} {:db/id 17592186230047 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230178 :tutorial/content "So far, our guesses for the particular solution have worked because the forcing term did not already appear in the complementary solution.

Sometimes, however, the right-hand side of the differential equation has the same form as a term that appears in the complementary solution $y_c(x).$ When this happens, our usual guess for $y_p(x)$ fails because it duplicates part of the complementary solution and cannot produce a new solution.

In this situation, we must modify our guess by *multiplying it by $x.$* Specifically, if the forcing term has the form $K e^{kx}$ and the complementary solution contains a term like $Ae^{kx},$ then instead of guessing

$$
y_p(x) = \alpha e^{kx},
$$

we try

$$
y_p(x) = \alpha \boldsymbol{x} e^{kx}.
$$

This works because multiplying by $x$ creates a new function that is *linearly independent* of the complementary solution. As a result, our guess no longer overlaps with $y_c(x)$ and can serve as a valid particular solution. We'll discuss linear independence of functions in more detail in future lessons.

Let’s see how this works in practice using a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "e6655774-c9ab-58c6-bfec-5013b08b7918" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14450 :tutorial/title "Cases When the Forcing Term is Part of the Complementary Solution"} :step/id #uuid "b7dc2094-d676-591f-98e7-87919cdf8889" :step/math-academy-id 597445 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230048}} {:db/id 17592186230048 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230229 :tutorial/content "Consider the differential equation

$$
y' + 5y = 10e^{-5x}.
$$

The associated homogeneous equation is

$$
y' + 5y = 0
$$

and so the complementary solution is 

$$
y_c(x) = Ae^{-5x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant. 

Notice that the forcing term is $f(x) = 10 e^{-5x},$ and yet $e^{-5x}$ is a term in the complementary solution. So, in this case, we assume a particular solution that takes the form 

$$
y_p(x) = \alpha x  e ^ {-5 x} ,
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

We calculate the first derivative of $y_p$ using the product rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{'} & =(\alpha x{e}^{-5x})^{'} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{-5x})^{'} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{-5x}-5x{e}^{-5x}) \\  & =\alpha (1-5x){e}^{-5x}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute $y_p$ and $y_p'$ into the differential equation and solve for $\alpha.$

$$
\begin{aligned}(\alpha (1-5x){e}^{-5x})+5\alpha x{e}^{-5x} & =10{e}^{-5x} \\ (1-5x+5x)\alpha {e}^{-5x} & =10{e}^{-5x} \\ \alpha {e}^{-5x} & =10{e}^{-5x} \\ \alpha  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution $y_p(x)$ is

$$
y_p(x) = 10x  e ^ {-5x}
$$

and thus the general solution to the equation is

$$
y(x) = y_c(x) + y_p(x) = Ae^{-5x} + 10xe^{-5x}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c5cb7b6d-2997-5082-a597-8a0e6e4eaf5b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14703 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "11a3780c-c51f-5b21-bfc3-9b6034b2e639" Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "62cac4a5-105b-5e43-8d88-63ce73a86e94" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14700 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "c3a6d6f6-44d9-519b-8417-7113691d787c" :step/math-academy-id 597440 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230046}} {:db/id 17592186230227 :tutorial/content "Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac {\textrm{d} y} {\textrm{d} x} + 3 y = 4 e ^ {2x}.
$$

The associated homogeneous equation is

$$
\frac {\textrm{d} y} {\textrm{d} x} + 3 y = 0
$$

and therefore, the complementary solution is 

$$
y_c(x) =  A e^{-3x},
$$

 

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant. Let's now find the **particular solution** $y_p(x)$ to this equation.

Since the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is the exponential function $f(x) = 4 e^{2x},$ and this is not incorporated within the complementary solution, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(x) = \alpha e^{2x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of $y_p$ gives

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y_p}{\textrm{d}x} = 2\alpha e ^{2x}.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute $y_p$ and $y_p'$ into the differential equation and solve for $\alpha{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(2\alpha {e}^{2x})+3(\alpha {e}^{2x}) & =4{e}^{2x} \\ (2+3)\alpha {e}^{2x} & =4{e}^{2x} \\ 5\alpha {e}^{2x} & =4{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution $y_p(x)$ is

$$
y_p(x) = \dfrac{4}{5} e ^{2x}.
$$

Finally, the **general solution** is given by

$$
y = y_c + y_p = A e^{-3x} + \dfrac{4}{5} e ^{2x}.
$$

We can employ a similar strategy when the forcing function is a sum of exponential functions. In this situation, we must modify our guess by *multiplying it by $x.$* Specifically, if the forcing term has the form $K e^{kx}$ and the complementary solution contains a term like $Ae^{kx},$ then instead of guessing

$$

$$

we try

$$
y_p(x) = \alpha \boldsymbol{x} e^{kx}.
$$

This works because multiplying by $x$ creates a new function that is *linearly independent* of the complementary solution. $$

The associated homogeneous equation is

and so the complementary solution is

Notice that the forcing term is $f(x) = 10 e^{-5x},$ and yet $e^{-5x}$ is a term in the complementary solution. So, in this case, we assume a particular solution that takes the form 

$$
y_p(x) = \alpha x  e ^ {-5 x} ,
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

We calculate the first derivative of $y_p$ using the product rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{'} & =(\alpha x{e}^{-5x})^{'} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{-5x})^{'} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{-5x}-5x{e}^{-5x}) \\  & =\alpha (1-5x){e}^{-5x}\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, the particular solution $y_p(x)$ is

$$
y_p(x) = 10x  e ^ {-5x}
$$

and thus the general solution to the equation is

$$
y(x) = y_c(x) + y_p(x) = Ae^{-5x} + 10xe^{-5x}.

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{7x},

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha x{e}^{7x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{7x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{7x}+7x{e}^{7x}) \\  & =\alpha (1+7x){e}^{7x}.\end{aligned}

17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ac389cb5-50b0-5d9d-9387-c7be6e7524a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-122352" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at $x=1\,m$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/f0/f08c9d1e8dce3c0ae7c37719cadc3fc60bf5de3030ce8c44ca7528a98f3abf7e.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -8{e}^{1-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8{e}^{0}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =16{e}^{1-x} \\ v & =\pm 4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4{e}^{(1-x)/2} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{(1-x)/2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=1$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{(x-1)/2}=2t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+1 \\ \frac{x-1}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x-1 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)+1.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "03c63cb6-dfb8-5730-962f-2e6452481748"} {:db/id 17592186420430 :step/content {:db/id 17592186256613 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "016a3368-f9d5-58aa-ab05-aad63edb1b18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(x)={x}^{2}+x+2" :db/id 17592186253680} {:answer/id #uuid "1e97ff28-e0bb-54b7-b8b3-9417ec6fd261" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(x)=\sqrt{2({x}^{2}+x+6)}" :db/id 17592186253929} {:answer/id #uuid "2371f7e7-c2e4-57e1-bd77-d71c072ed039" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+x+2}" :db/id 17592186253988} {:answer/id #uuid "bb5e00e1-832f-5f55-83f9-b8c48153a1c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(x)=\frac{4}{3}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+6}" :db/id 17592186255339} {:answer/id #uuid "fbf76d94-8303-5033-a055-32483b709927" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(x)={x}^{2}+3x" :db/id 17592186255884}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186253929} :answer-field/id #uuid "7a51decc-a151-5408-9864-1176626e3665" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186256148}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4bd8ece4-afaf-5640-9ad2-c2e8ef66ae37" :question/math-academy-id "q-122338" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/98/983beaf02582c5ebaee129e28bba657eb2db5e4da7f74eb4b8eba73b9083a259.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2x+1.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2x+1.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (2x+1)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}+x+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={1}^{2}+1+C \\ 8 & =2+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+x+6 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+x+6) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+x+6)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{2({x}^{2}+x+6)}.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=1\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =\frac{8}{(0+2)^{4}}+K \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{16}{(x+2)^{4}} \\ v & =\pm \frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}} \\ (x+2)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int (x+2)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int (x+2)^{2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{3}(x+2)^{3} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+2)^{3} & =12t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=8,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+2)^{3}=12t+8.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{3} & =12t+8 \\ x+2 & =\sqrt[3]{12t+8} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{12t+8}-2.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a1a065d0-24c6-5622-ba75-1f337d376e40" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420429}} {:db/id 17592186420433 :step/content {:db/id 17592186256616 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "55e5f7fd-5f39-54d0-b24b-d6386ba4b120" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(x)={2}^{3-x}" :db/id 17592186254422} {:answer/id #uuid "7715943a-4b29-5731-aa1b-21b6a9f5bcda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(x)={2}^{1-x}+3" :db/id 17592186254725} {:answer/id #uuid "7a7f8494-68d3-5ece-b55e-5a21d83663af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(x)=2\sqrt{3\cdot {2}^{1-x}+1}" :db/id 17592186254759} {:answer/id #uuid "bbaa6296-4ac5-5e74-907b-e485c987c549" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(x)=2\sqrt{{2}^{1-x}+3}" :db/id 17592186255345} {:answer/id #uuid "cfa68c5c-78bd-533d-9a2b-0493c8ac2f7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(x)=\frac{4}{3}\sqrt{{2}^{3-x}+5}" :db/id 17592186255520}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186255345} :answer-field/id #uuid "6837870e-c4ce-53d3-8d92-89b9b7c8217b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186256116}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9efcc68b-3929-5bf9-ab56-4c19b9a57740" :question/math-academy-id "q-122341" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is ${2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,{m/s}^{2}$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/6d/6ddbfef68a0b41a6ee3f11c46ff7821f7ff0dc23a16b4244b5e7a1f6579d7dd2.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude ${2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-{2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-{2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-{2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={2}^{2-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={2}^{2-x}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={2}^{2-1}+C \\ 8 & =2+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={2}^{2-x}+6 \\ {v}^{2} & ={2}^{3-x}+12 \\ {v}^{2} & =4({2}^{1-x}+3) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{{2}^{1-x}+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2\sqrt{{2}^{1-x}+3}.

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8{e}^{0}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =16{e}^{1-x} \\ v & =\pm 4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.\end{aligned}

from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/98/983beaf02582c5ebaee129e28bba657eb2db5e4da7f74eb4b8eba73b9083a259.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2x+1.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2x+1.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (2x+1)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}+x+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={1}^{2}+1+C \\ 8 & =2+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+x+6 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+x+6) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+x+6)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{2({x}^{2}+x+6)}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5b4469a6-0f97-5a60-8a7e-bd0dcb2520b2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420433}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "016a3368-f9d5-58aa-ab05-aad63edb1b18" :answer/type {:db/id $$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-{2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-{2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-{2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={2}^{2-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={2}^{2-x}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={2}^{2-1}+C \\ 8 & =2+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={2}^{2-x}+6 \\ {v}^{2} & ={2}^{3-x}+12 \\ {v}^{2} & =4({2}^{1-x}+3) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{{2}^{1-x}+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2\sqrt{{2}^{1-x}+3}.

"![](images/14/141c6dd6c91841238298b86fac1063c76faeb7cd103e13d2723f6ac05ed58f50.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=1\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =\frac{8}{(0+2)^{4}}+K \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{16}{(x+2)^{4}} \\ v & =\pm \frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}} \\ (x+2)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int (x+2)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int (x+2)^{2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{3}(x+2)^{3} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+2)^{3} & =12t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=8,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+2)^{3}=12t+8.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{3} & =12t+8 \\ x+2 & =\sqrt[3]{12t+8} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{12t+8}-2.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a1a065d0-24c6-5622-ba75-1f337d376e40" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420429}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4364ff09-2922-52f1-bb5f-e67a3ba34a6f" :answer/type {:db/id "8d544f0e-e224-5a8f-b2d9-7d23deb9a689" :question/math-academy-id "q-122347" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is ${3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3\,{m/s}^{2}$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $v=-2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=1\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place." :question/worked-solution "![](images/3c/3c5450b18c5dc58b082faadf4086b6a21c0c9b55afb016090147609a2ccfe719.png)

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-{3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-{3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int [-{3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3]\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={3}^{1-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=-2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(-2\sqrt{2})^{2} & ={3}^{1-2}+C \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{3}+C \\ C & =\frac{11}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3} \\ {v}^{2} & =2({3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3}) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v=-\sqrt{2({3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3})}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =-\sqrt{2({3}^{1-1}+\frac{11}{3})} \\  & =-\sqrt{\frac{28}{3}} \\  & ≈-3.1\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place."} :step/id #uuid "a96f26a1-150f-53aa-92db-8203a5d7c383"} {:db/id 17592186437147 :step/content {:db/id 17592186256600 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c5b2eeb-074d-51bf-9b3f-10803e274c41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x+1}" :db/id 17592186253770} {:answer/id #uuid "56351265-a52c-5206-885d-fa5dfeb276eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x+1}" :db/id 17592186254428} {:answer/id #uuid "afa87942-4e3f-5a55-ae5f-5d22dd94cb53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{x+1}" :db/id 17592186255214} {:answer/id #uuid "d4b91cfd-f727-572e-865c-a94f7aba262d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}^{2}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{x+1}" :db/id 17592186255559} {:answer/id #uuid "e6bf1029-4403-54dd-a55a-c9e8275e658a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{x+1}" :db/id 17592186255702}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186255702} :answer-field/id #uuid "b673d4fe-7d5a-50cb-99f3-481a645a95f1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186256249}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a2aa7557-417c-5f06-bca6-b63a94c74ba4" :question/math-academy-id "q-122307" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $\frac{1}{x+1}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?" :question/worked-solution "![](images/47/473a3f91d91351499d5849ee07a86cfcfc2b257949d6ebba68b3261201f2bf68.png)

$$

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${e}^{x/2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{x/2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={e}^{x/2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{e}^{x/2}+C.
$$

Now, since  $v=\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{5})^{2} & =2{e}^{0/2}+C \\ \frac{5}{2} & =2+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{x/2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ {v}^{2} & =4{e}^{x/2}+1 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4{e}^{x/2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4{e}^{x/2}+1}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4{e}^{1/2}+1} \\ v & =\sqrt{4\sqrt{e}+1} \\  & ≈2.8\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place."} :step/id #uuid "f9498a14-80ad-5194-bc2c-7090bc99b1db" :step/next {:db/id 17592186437146}}] :activity/title "Velocity and Acceleration as Functions of Displacement" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186437145} {:db/id 17592186437149 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167089 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ebf18ee-af52-58eb-9db4-f851658ecd7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+t)" :db/id 17592186253931} {:answer/id #uuid "1f068fc2-f6b1-5e9e-af2b-751b98bcdc5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(t)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+t)" :db/id 17592186253936} {:answer/id #uuid "49f209c9-1626-5df5-aefb-bdf07e8a5715" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(t)=\frac{1}{2}t" :db/id 17592186254305} {:answer/id #uuid "de5cdbb3-0dd8-544a-8444-7a6932630c5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(t)=1-{e}^{t}" :db/id 17592186255642} {:answer/id #uuid "e35e425f-e29f-5937-be75-0ebb5ff34e95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(t)={e}^{t}-1" :db/id 17592186255683}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186255683} :answer-field/id #uuid "877a8eaf-76c0-5b50-a12d-6f6b23536812" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186256174}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8488fc53-7024-5b0e-acc8-a7217b9f9e03" :question/math-academy-id "q-122170" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, the velocity is given by $v(x)=(1+x)\,m/s.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/a8/a8a6f49ead700bee856b1bbdbb10848eac0a57609da14e3967916a36eb56f048.png)

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-{3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-{3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int [-{3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3]\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={3}^{1-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=-2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(-2\sqrt{2})^{2} & ={3}^{1-2}+C \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{3}+C \\ C & =\frac{11}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3} \\ {v}^{2} & =2({3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3}) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v=-\sqrt{2({3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3})}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =-\sqrt{2({3}^{1-1}+\frac{11}{3})} \\  & =-\sqrt{\frac{28}{3}} \\  & ≈-3.1\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place."} :step/id #uuid "a96f26a1-150f-53aa-92db-8203a5d7c383"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8658c0bb-cfd4-5142-bbcb-e4097359b029" :answer/type {:db/id Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${e}^{x/2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{x/2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={e}^{x/2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{e}^{x/2}+C.
$$

Now, since  $v=\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{5})^{2} & =2{e}^{0/2}+C \\ \frac{5}{2} & =2+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{x/2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ {v}^{2} & =4{e}^{x/2}+1 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4{e}^{x/2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4{e}^{x/2}+1}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4{e}^{1/2}+1} \\ v & =\sqrt{4\sqrt{e}+1} \\  & ≈2.8\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/math-academy-id 2131} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134811 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135102 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2,$ expressed in terms of its component functions as

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

If the first partial derivatives of $P$ and $Q$ exist, then the **divergence** of $\mathbf F,$ denoted $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F,$ is the scalar given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

Notice that if we define the differential operator $\nabla$ (a.k.a. the "del" operator) as 

$$
\nabla =  \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} +  \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y},
$$

 

then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is given by the dot product

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F.
$$

For example, suppose that the vector field $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = 2xy\, \mathbf i + e^{yx} \, \mathbf j .
$$

Then, we can calculate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}$ using the dot product formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =∇\cdot F \\  & =(i\,\frac{∂}{∂x}+j\,\frac{∂}{∂y})\cdot (2xy\,i+{e}^{yx}\,j) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{yx}) \\  & =2y+x{e}^{yx}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "086f12c3-0ab5-54ed-8b4e-5c70e8c7c7e5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5116 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5c2a161a-d267-5999-8795-ba9baba0146f" :step/math-academy-id #uuid "eb39b82a-9c43-56ff-9c10-70ad9f735fab" :step/math-academy-id 33322} {:db/id 17592186134842 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135114 :tutorial/content "Our goal now is to develop an intuitive understanding of what the divergence of a vector field measures.

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ and the point $S,$ shown below. Imagine that this vector field represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. 

![](images/a7/a785c84976242d699af11ab2203600e2007e95e35b60665ba9882c8f0f25bce3.png)

 

We can see from our diagram that $S$ acts like a **source**. You can think of this as an open faucet, pushing water onto the plane and away from itself. 

Since $S$ acts like a source, $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is nonzero. By convention, if a point $S$ acts like a source, the divergence is positive:

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0
$$

In this particular case, *every* point in our vector field acts as a source. So $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0$ everywhere.

If we reverse the situation, we get the following:

![](images/b4/b4c923bbde36568e4e2f36f7d388622a520d0799d558049f72d0194e0bd679f7.png)

 

We can see from our diagram that $T$ acts like a **sink**. You can think of this as an open plughole that sucks in the surrounding water.

Since $T$ acts like a sink, $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is also nonzero. By convention, if a point $T$ acts like a sink, the divergence is negative:

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0
$$

Every point in our vector field acts like a sink in this case. So $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0$ everywhere.

Finally, note that if $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = 0$ everywhere in the domain of some vector field $\mathbf F,$ we say that $\mathbf F$ is **solenoidal.**" :tutorial/id #uuid "a2cdf73b-116c-5cf4-a5a2-a8c95e447127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5518 :tutorial/title "Physical Interpretation of Divergence"} :step/id #uuid "6a9298c4-106a-569c-bd0b-5d24d3e71b0f" :step/math-academy-id 34359 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134848}} {:db/id 17592186134844 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133889 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133705 :question/id #uuid "3cbc5b4a-dde4-59b0-bc34-08c4d8776e0e" :question/math-academy-id "e-9489"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e6b79409-5a5b-533b-8d46-4e0e6d963b3a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134065} {:db/id 17592186134369} {:db/id 17592186235535} {:db/id 17592186259486} {:db/id 17592186259487} {:db/id 17592186259490} {:db/id 17592186266056} {:db/id 17592186266057} {:db/id 17592186266058} {:db/id 17592186362524} {:db/id 17592186383041} {:db/id 17592186385415} {:db/id 17592186407632} {:db/id 17592186424230} {:db/id 17592186436933} {:db/id 17592186436934}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Three Dimensions"} :step/id #uuid "77b5a013-eab6-50c3-9f63-2a51f2e967b2" :step/math-academy-id 35525 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134842}} {:db/id 17592186134848 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135120 :tutorial/content "The following two vector fields behave either as a source or a sink. Therefore, they both have divergence.

![](images/93/939efa85ebfe4805a27595b60a797b8a3435075590ee77f7a18d04bd76d91f1a.png)

The following vector fields are solenoidal (i.e., they each have zero divergence).

![](images/ed/edb2f908fa78439bf985b5754c9fcc5968c21926dbe124297b67af046a9f70a3.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ddbe7ae2-caaf-5436-b1c7-aabc0eec115d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5793 :tutorial/title "Examples of Vector Field With Divergence and Solenoidal Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "88b27d23-7358-51e8-9457-a8b063ed5a52" :step/math-academy-id 35536 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134826}} {:db/id 17592186134849 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135121 :tutorial/content "There are a few things we should note about the divergence:

- We can only compute the divergence of a *vector* field, and a vector field's divergence is a *scalar* field. So if $G(x,y) = \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F,$ then we have the following map:

$$
\underbrace{\,\,\,\mathbf F(x,y)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{vector field}} \mapsto\underbrace{\,\,\,G(x,y)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{scalar field}}
$$

In contrast, if $f(x,y)$ is a scalar field, then the statement $\textrm{div}\, f$ has no meaning.

- We can easily extend the notion of divergence to three dimensions. So, if $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j + R\,\mathbf k,$ then $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z},
$$

where the three-dimensional differential operator $\nabla$ is given by

$$
\nabla =  \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} +  \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y} + \mathbf k\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}.
$$

- The divergence of a vector field at a point $P$ gives us helpful information about the tendency of the vector field to behave like a source or a sink at $P.$ We'll describe this in more detail shortly." :tutorial/id #uuid "9b8de083-51c2-581b-ad36-a773dca8af05" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5794 :tutorial/title "Some Important Notes About the Divergence of a Vector Field"} :step/id #uuid "e856caa2-317e-5779-b004-597af558a506" :step/math-academy-id 35537 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134822}}] :activity/title "The Divergence of a Vector Field" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134010} {:db/id 17592186134811 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135102 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2,$ expressed in terms of its component functions as

\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0
$$

Every point in our vector field acts like a sink in this case. So $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0$ everywhere.

Finally, note that if $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = 0$ everywhere in the domain of some vector field $\mathbf F,$ we say that $\mathbf F$ is **solenoidal.**" :tutorial/id #uuid "a2cdf73b-116c-5cf4-a5a2-a8c95e447127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5518 :tutorial/title "Physical Interpretation of Divergence"} :step/id #uuid "6a9298c4-106a-569c-bd0b-5d24d3e71b0f" :step/math-academy-id 34359 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134848}} {:db/id 17592186135114 :tutorial/content "Our goal now is to develop an intuitive understanding of what the divergence of a vector field measures.

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ and the point $S,$ shown below. Imagine that this vector field represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. 

![](images/a7/a785c84976242d699af11ab2203600e2007e95e35b60665ba9882c8f0f25bce3.png)

 

We can see from our diagram that $S$ acts like a **source**. You can think of this as an open faucet, pushing water onto the plane and away from itself. 

Since $S$ acts like a source, $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is nonzero. By convention, if a point $S$ acts like a source, the divergence is positive:

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0
$$

In this particular case, *every* point in our vector field acts as a source. So $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0$ everywhere.

If we reverse the situation, we get the following:

![](images/b4/b4c923bbde36568e4e2f36f7d388622a520d0799d558049f72d0194e0bd679f7.png)

 

We can see from our diagram that $T$ acts like a **sink**. You can think of this as an open plughole that sucks in the surrounding water.

Since $T$ acts like a sink, $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is also nonzero. By convention, if a point $T$ acts like a sink, the divergence is negative:

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0
$$

Every point in our vector field acts like a sink in this case. So $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0$ everywhere.

Finally, note that if $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = 0$ everywhere in the domain of some vector field $\mathbf F,$ we say that $\mathbf F$ is **solenoidal.**" :tutorial/id #uuid "a2cdf73b-116c-5cf4-a5a2-a8c95e447127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5518 :tutorial/title "Physical Interpretation of Divergence"} {:db/id 17592186134848 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135120 :tutorial/content "The following two vector fields behave either as a source or a sink. ![](images/93/939efa85ebfe4805a27595b60a797b8a3435075590ee77f7a18d04bd76d91f1a.png)

The following vector fields are solenoidal (i.e., they each have zero divergence).

![](images/ed/edb2f908fa78439bf985b5754c9fcc5968c21926dbe124297b67af046a9f70a3.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ddbe7ae2-caaf-5436-b1c7-aabc0eec115d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5793 :tutorial/title "Examples of Vector Field With Divergence and Solenoidal Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "88b27d23-7358-51e8-9457-a8b063ed5a52" :step/math-academy-id 35536 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134826}} {:db/id 17592186135120 :tutorial/content "The following two vector fields behave either as a source or a sink. Therefore, they both have divergence.

![](images/93/939efa85ebfe4805a27595b60a797b8a3435075590ee77f7a18d04bd76d91f1a.png)

The following vector fields are solenoidal (i.e., they each have zero divergence).

![](images/ed/edb2f908fa78439bf985b5754c9fcc5968c21926dbe124297b67af046a9f70a3.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ddbe7ae2-caaf-5436-b1c7-aabc0eec115d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5793 :tutorial/title "Examples of Vector Field With Divergence and Solenoidal Vector Fields"} {:db/id 17592186135121 :tutorial/content "There are a few things we should note about the divergence:

- We can only compute the divergence of a *vector* field, and a vector field's divergence is a *scalar* field. So if $G(x,y) = \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F,$ then we have the following map:

$$
\underbrace{\,\,\,\mathbf F(x,y)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{vector field}} \mapsto\underbrace{\,\,\,G(x,y)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{scalar field}}
$$

In contrast, if $f(x,y)$ is a scalar field, then the statement $\textrm{div}\, f$ has no meaning.

- We can easily extend the notion of divergence to three dimensions. So, if $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j + R\,\mathbf k,$ then $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z},
$$

where the three-dimensional differential operator $\nabla$ is given by

$$
\nabla =  \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} +  \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y} + \mathbf k\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}.
$$

- The divergence of a vector field at a point $P$ gives us helpful information about the tendency of the vector field to behave like a source or a sink at $P.$ We'll describe this in more detail shortly." :tutorial/id #uuid "9b8de083-51c2-581b-ad36-a773dca8af05" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5794 :tutorial/title "Some Important Notes About the Divergence of a Vector Field"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186407634} :activity/id #uuid "23bb149c-27d7-5070-88b1-a3124f094ad2" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049459 :topic/id #uuid "f6fd4776-56f0-5112-9cdc-83e344004d93" :topic/math-academy-id 2131} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186407633 :step/content {:db/id 17592186407632 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08e054f8-7842-51d9-944e-506f086c64ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2-\pi " :db/id 17592186407614} {:answer/id #uuid "30bd69d5-9aed-5f53-bd57-88c0d8b71e93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186407615} {:answer/id #uuid "951b5e1a-06b7-5f54-b81b-2e7935528e41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\pi " :db/id 17592186407621} {:answer/id #uuid "b2537554-7ead-5776-b7ea-b0a5c6ea2d72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-\pi " :db/id 17592186407622} {:answer/id #uuid "de576d13-a320-57ea-81fe-65cb1f522e77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+\pi " :db/id 17592186407625}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407614} :answer-field/id #uuid "55f12593-79dd-5e1b-8574-a974a94bfc5a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186407628}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f48c368c-417f-5ffe-9791-056b549ac545" :question/math-academy-id "q-105559" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F=\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x\,i+y\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y\,j+{e}^{2z}\,k.$ 
Evaluate $∇\cdot F$ at the point $(0,1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
∇\cdot F=\text{div}\,F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{2z}) \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi x+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y+\pi y\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y+2{e}^{2z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(0,1,0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(0,1,0) & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+2{e}^{0} \\  & =0+0-\pi +2 \\  & =2-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1d73206f-cfb2-5389-b819-954a52ec5c0a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186407635}} {:db/id 17592186407634 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134065 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6c79d74f-4409-57e4-b361-e941cc41aa8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3y{z}^{2}" :db/id 17592186407618} {:answer/id #uuid "941fb884-9dbd-5e6e-bdb3-9c13326a2f3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3y{z}^{2}" :db/id 17592186407620} {:answer/id #uuid "d9966256-2b26-5637-969d-ec652f55ff58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{xy}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{z}^{3}" :db/id 17592186407624} {:answer/id #uuid "ec0916bb-4bf2-5bfb-8625-f74c2a28d4bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{xy}\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j+{z}^{3}\,k" :db/id 17592186407626} {:answer/id #uuid "eecb625e-fb38-58c5-8c7d-425f0374e2c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{y}\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,j+3y{z}^{2}\,k" :db/id 17592186407627}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407618} :answer-field/id #uuid "fafbd1ee-fb02-5785-b3f4-4426b308c48e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186407630}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "db7680f4-57f3-5a1a-a81a-52c92b75f829" :question/math-academy-id "q-105555" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\,i-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j+y{z}^{3}\,k.$

:question/math-academy-id "q-105572" :question/problem "![](images/58/584016c88e5916984e181118d52caab95dba1fd0d861e0fd248a4e023d1b07da.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{div}\,F=0$
- **II.** $\text{div}\,F>0$
- **III.** $\text{div}\,F<0$
- **IV.** $F$ is solenoidal" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement III is true, whereas statements I and II are false. Notice that the lengths of the vectors decrease as we move horizontally and vertically towards the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a sink at every point.

- Statement IV is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} :step/id #uuid "84dd7364-713d-5340-9f9c-2da553617182"}] :activity/title "The Divergence of a Vector Field" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186407612} {:db/id 17592186407634 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134065 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6c79d74f-4409-57e4-b361-e941cc41aa8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3y{z}^{2}" :db/id 17592186407618} {:answer/id #uuid "941fb884-9dbd-5e6e-bdb3-9c13326a2f3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3y{z}^{2}" :db/id 17592186407620} {:answer/id #uuid "d9966256-2b26-5637-969d-ec652f55ff58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{xy}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{z}^{3}" :db/id 17592186407624} {:answer/id #uuid "ec0916bb-4bf2-5bfb-8625-f74c2a28d4bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{xy}\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j+{z}^{3}\,k" :db/id 17592186407626} {:answer/id #uuid "eecb625e-fb38-58c5-8c7d-425f0374e2c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{y}\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,j+3y{z}^{2}\,k" :db/id 17592186407627}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407618} :answer-field/id #uuid "fafbd1ee-fb02-5785-b3f4-4426b308c48e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186407630}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "db7680f4-57f3-5a1a-a81a-52c92b75f829" :question/math-academy-id "q-105555" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\,i-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j+y{z}^{3}\,k.$

- **II.** $\text{div}\,F>0$
- **III.** $\text{div}\,F<0$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement III is true, whereas statements I and II are false. Notice that the lengths of the vectors decrease as we move horizontally and vertically towards the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a sink at every point.

- Statement IV is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

:question/math-academy-id "q-105575" :question/problem "![](images/11/11d38951b884f17616a61403d793322d0e2ea28910e806fe8f018251508352a1.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $∇\cdot F=0$

- **II.** $∇\cdot F>0$

- **III.** $∇\cdot F<0$

- **IV.** $F$ is solenoidal" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- **III.** $∇\cdot F<0$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement III is true, whereas statements I and II are false. Notice that the lengths of the vector's $x$-components decrease as we move horizontally towards the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a sink at every point.

- Statement IV is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

:question/math-academy-id "q-131196" :question/problem "![](images/4b/4bf8de7e8719545b3d8abf5dc9fb4bc0c5f71034dba7186b7d9822d9e8be044d.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $∇\cdot F=0$

- **II.** $∇\cdot F>0$

- **III.** $∇\cdot F<0$

- **IV.** $F$ is solenoidal" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement III is true, whereas statements I and II are false. Notice that the lengths of the vector's $x$-components decrease as we move horizontally towards the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a sink at every point.

- Statement IV is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} :step/id #uuid "c4ea5422-7fe4-544c-96ca-1a8f6b528092"} {:db/id 17592186436936 :step/content {:db/id 17592186241080 :question/answer-fields - **II.** $∇\cdot F>0$

- **III.** $∇\cdot F<0$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

- Statement I is true, whereas statements II and III are false. For any point $P,$ the sum of the inward-pointing vectors equals the sum of the outward-pointing vectors. Therefore, $F$ acts neither like a source nor a sink.

- Statement IV is true. Since $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere, the vector field $F$ is solenoidal.

$$
∇\cdot F=\text{div}\,F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2x})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y{e}^{2x})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(-z{e}^{2x}) \\  & =2{e}^{2x}-{e}^{2x}-{e}^{2x} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "af33c61a-5271-559b-9054-88db8d041045" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436935}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "13a914c9-ac5b-510b-8770-498ebbd342d6" :answer/type {:db/id want to evaluate the repeated integral

$$
\int_{0}^{1}\int_{x}^{2x} (x-2y) \ \mathrm{d}  y \ \mathrm{d}  x.
$$

Notice that the domain of integration is a type I region. 

To compute this integral, we must bear the following important points in mind.

- We start with the inner integral, as usual.

- When integrating with respect to $y,$ we treat $x$ as though it were a constant.

- The limits of integration for the inner integral are functions of $x.$ Once again, we treat $x$ as though it were a constant and substitute the integration limits as usual. After this step, there should be no more $y$'s in our integral.

- Finally, we compute the outer integral.

Let's apply these steps to solve the given problem.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{x}^{2x}(x-2y)\text{ }dy]\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[xy-{y}^{2}]_{x}^{2x}\text{ }dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x\cdot (2x)-{(2x)}^{2}]-[x\cdot (x)-(x)^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[2{x}^{2}-4{x}^{2}]-[{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx & =-2{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{[{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}[{1}^{3}-{0}^{3}] \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3698e7e3-4bc2-5db0-96b5-172131284b4a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4262 :tutorial/title "Evaluating Repeated Integrals With Variable Limits"} :step/id #uuid
