Then, we simplify.

$$
\begin{aligned} (x - 3)(x^2 - 2x + 6) \\ &= x(x^2 - 2x + 6) - 3(x^2 - 2x + 6) \\ &= x^3 - 2x^2 + 6x - 3x^2 + 6x - 18 \\ &= x^3 - 5x^2 + 12x - 18 \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064957 :question/id #uuid "52095cdc-6970-5a9e-9cc9-29593a4509ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-78044"} {:db/id 17592186064958 :question/id #uuid "739a88f1-53d5-509c-9f14-a0b415758a8e" :question/math-academy-id "q-78045"} {:db/id 17592186233791 :question/id #uuid "76a8faca-c056-5acc-8cda-bb43a948af4e" :question/math-academy-id "q-31385" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064276 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "43f97f24-06a1-50cc-9c73-48bc491c632f" :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying a Binomial and a Quadratic Trinomial"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $(3x+4)({x}^{2}-6x-9)?$" :question/worked-solution "We distribute both terms of the binomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x+4)({x}^{2}-6x-9) & = \\ 3x({x}^{2}-6x-9)+4({x}^{2}-6x-9) & = \\ 3{x}^{3}-18{x}^{2}-27x+4{x}^{2}-24x-36 & = \\ 3{x}^{3}-14{x}^{2}-51x-36\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186234404 :question/id #uuid "ca8f6868-f485-5407-858b-66b9b3950355" :question/math-academy-id "q-78167"} {:db/id 17592186064277 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064120 :question/id #uuid "55f28c00-cfe7-507e-830f-f7d993d16687" :question/math-academy-id "e-6710"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f7019d52-33a1-5968-9a93-2f2f06fbb0d6" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064677 :question/id #uuid "c5bf28e7-0c5f-59ac-9be6-97c2c00faf63" :question/math-academy-id "q-2676"} {:db/id 17592186064959 :question/id #uuid "232f7662-1406-54d6-9c25-c5564003c163" :question/math-academy-id "q-78046"} {:db/id 17592186233141 :question/id #uuid "e08294c6-a979-573d-8467-4eac7fae6a3e" :question/math-academy-id "q-111362"} {:db/id 17592186234405 :question/id #uuid "4ce674de-c42a-508a-99bd-3e2090e8e038" :question/math-academy-id "q-78174"}] :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying Trinomials"} {:db/id 17592186064120 :question/id #uuid "55f28c00-cfe7-507e-830f-f7d993d16687" :question/math-academy-id "e-6710" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186064277 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f7019d52-33a1-5968-9a93-2f2f06fbb0d6" :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying Trinomials"}] :question/problem "Given that $(3s^2 + 2s - 1)(s^2 + s + 2) = 3s^4 + \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{a}s^3 + \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{b}s^2 + \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{c}s - 2$, calculate $a+b+c$." :question/worked-solution "We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify.

$$
\begin{aligned}
(3s^{2} + 2s - 1)(s^{2} + s + 2) &=  \\
3s^{2}(s^{2} + s + 2) + 2s(s^{2} + s + 2) + (-1)(s^{2} + s + 2) &=  \\
3s^{4} + 3s^{3} + 6s^{2} + 2s^{3} + 2s^{2} + 4s - s^{2} - s - 2 &=  \\
&= 3s^{4} + 5s^{3} + 7s^{2} + 3s - 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Matching up the coefficients, we find that $a=5$, $b=7$, and $c=3$.

So, we have

$$
a + b + c = 5 + 7 + 3 = 15
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064677 :question/id #uuid "c5bf28e7-0c5f-59ac-9be6-97c2c00faf63" :question/math-academy-id "q-2676"} {:db/id 17592186064959 :question/id #uuid "232f7662-1406-54d6-9c25-c5564003c163" :question/math-academy-id "q-78046"} {:db/id 17592186233141 :question/id #uuid "e08294c6-a979-573d-8467-4eac7fae6a3e" :question/math-academy-id "q-111362"} {:db/id 17592186234405 :question/id #uuid "4ce674de-c42a-508a-99bd-3e2090e8e038" :question/math-academy-id "q-78174" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064277 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f7019d52-33a1-5968-9a93-2f2f06fbb0d6" :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying Trinomials"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Given that  $(3{w}^{2}+w+5)({w}^{2}+w+1)=3{w}^{4}+a{w}^{3}+b{w}^{2}+cw+5,$ calculate $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3{w}^{2}+w+5)({w}^{2}+w+1) & = \\ 3{w}^{2}({w}^{2}+w+1)+w({w}^{2}+w+1)+5({w}^{2}+w+1) & = \\ 3{w}^{4}+3{w}^{3}+3{w}^{2}+{w}^{3}+{w}^{2}+w+5{w}^{2}+5w+5 & = \\ 3{w}^{4}+4{w}^{3}+9{w}^{2}+6w+5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=4,$ $b=9,$ and $c=6.$ So, 

$$
a+b+c=4+9+6=19.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064278 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064121 :question/id #uuid "9e77dab4-4e8b-51df-a070-1a42fcdbf212" :question/math-academy-id "e-6711"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "09357892-5d4b-5346-99b0-9babc7b0d574" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064736 :question/id #uuid "aa8dfac6-2e07-5a12-91bc-c7ca479ccc66" :question/math-academy-id "q-31382"} {:db/id 17592186064737 :question/id #uuid "9fa85edc-4b99-5e5d-a446-3d789169f619" :question/math-academy-id "q-31384"} {:db/id 17592186233706 :question/id #uuid "872c4f68-faa5-5619-88fd-07a441457df3" :question/math-academy-id "q-2744"} {:db/id 17592186233790 :question/id #uuid "3b98fea0-a66b-5248-90db-62d7c85781e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-31383"}] :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying Binomials and Trinomials Containing More Than One Variable"} {:db/id 17592186064121 :question/id #uuid "9e77dab4-4e8b-51df-a070-1a42fcdbf212" :question/math-academy-id "e-6711" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186064278 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "09357892-5d4b-5346-99b0-9babc7b0d574" :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying Binomials and Trinomials Containing More Than One Variable"}] :question/problem "What is the coefficient of $a^2b$ in the product $(a+b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)$?" :question/worked-solution "We distribute both terms of the binomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify.

$$
\begin{aligned}
(a + b)(a^{2} + ab + b^{2}) &=  \\
a(a^{2} + ab + b^{2}) + b(a^{2} + ab + b^{2}) &=  \\
a^{3} + a^{2}b + ab^{2} + a^{2}b + ab^{2} + b^{3} &=  \\
&= a^{3} + 2a^{2}b + 2ab^{2} + b^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coefficient of $a^2 b$ is $2$."} {:db/id 17592186064736 :question/id #uuid "aa8dfac6-2e07-5a12-91bc-c7ca479ccc66" :question/math-academy-id "q-31382"} {:db/id 17592186064737 :question/id #uuid "9fa85edc-4b99-5e5d-a446-3d789169f619" :question/math-academy-id "q-31384"} {:db/id 17592186233706 :question/id #uuid "872c4f68-faa5-5619-88fd-07a441457df3" :question/math-academy-id "q-2744"} {:db/id 17592186233790 :question/id #uuid "3b98fea0-a66b-5248-90db-62d7c85781e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-31383"} {:db/id 17592186049561} {:db/id 17592186049755} {:db/id 17592186049759} {:db/id 17592186050449} {:db/id 17592186051061} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186065162} :activity/id #uuid "0c7c191d-53bd-5ae5-94c5-4eed4a0e0009" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049500 :topic/id #uuid "f967432c-0e8a-553d-8497-053cde92d843" :topic/math-academy-id 361} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065162 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065375 :tutorial/content "To multiply a binomial and a trinomial, we take each term of the binomial and multiply it by every term in the trinomial. Then, we simplify by collecting like terms.

For example, to multiply $({\color{blue}{x}} + {\color{red}{3}})$ and $(x^2 + 2x+4)$, we multiply ${\color{blue}{x}}$ and $(x^2 + 2x+4)$, and then we add this to the product of ${\color{red}{3}}$ and $(x^2 + 2x+4)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}

the Formulas for Variation of Parameters"}] :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) =
A
\mathbf{x}(t) +
\mathbf{f}(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form $\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \mathbf{u}(t),$ where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for $\mathbf x_p(t)$ is given below. 

$\textrm{L1}{:}\:$ $\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \mathbf{u}(t)$

$\textrm{L2}{:}\:$ $\mathbf{x}'_p(t) = \Phi \mathbf{u}'(t) + \Phi' \mathbf{u}(t)$

$\textrm{L3}{:}\:$ $\Phi \mathbf{u}'(t) + \Phi' \mathbf{u}(t) = A \Phi \mathbf{u}(t) + \mathbf{f}(t)$

$\textrm{L4}{:}\:$ $\Phi' = A \Phi$

$\textrm{L5}{:}\:$ $\Phi \mathbf{u}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(t)$

$\textrm{L6}{:}\:$ $\mathbf{u}'(t) = \Phi^{-1}(t) \mathbf{f}(t)$

$\textrm{L7}{:}\:$ $\displaystyle\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t$

$\textrm{L8}{:}\:$ $\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \int \Phi^{-1}\mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t$

Fill in the blanks with the correct reasons to justify each step of the reasoning.

- We first consider line $\textrm{L4}.$ Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}'(t) =A\mathbf{x}(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $\mathbf{c}(t)$ of $\Phi$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
\mathbf{c}'(t) =A\mathbf{c}(t),
$$

where $\mathbf{c}'(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $\Phi.$ As a result, this means that $\Phi' = A \Phi.$ Therefore, $\textrm{L4}$ follows from the fact that ![](images/f3/f3cf7b9339acd3d9b370c67a182509bff354728494afda00e2e991f3a09996af.png) matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\textrm{L5}$ and $\textrm{L6}.$ Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $\Phi$ is invertible. Therefore, $\textrm{L6}$ follows from $\textrm{L5}$ by ![](images/8b/8ba4d14f89d4c90c90f84e0618b0cf8dedadbf2c3989cc9533e44590100357d1.png) both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\textrm{L1},$ $\textrm{L7},$ and $\textrm{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t
$$

from $\textrm{L7}$ into $\textrm{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167262 :question/id #uuid "f3e98464-6e85-513e-a930-d0947c1c72b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-336711"} {:db/id 17592186311738 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$

$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-2{e}^{-4t})-2{e}^{-4t}\cdot {e}^{3t}}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{3t} & -2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{t} \\ -\frac{17}{10}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{17}{10}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{3t} \\ -\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{2}t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=\frac{5}{2}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{5}{2}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{2}t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(\frac{5}{2}t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}\cdot (\frac{5}{2}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{5}{6}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{5}{6}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{5}{6}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{5}{18}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{5}{18}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-\frac{1}{2}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =(-\frac{1}{2}t)\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & 5{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{18}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}5(3t-1)+45(t+1) \\ 5(3t-1)+9(t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}30t+20 \\ 12t+2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

[{:db/id 17592186167896 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167991 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of ordinary differential equations

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) =
A
\mathbf{x}(t) +
\mathbf{f}(t)
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix and $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is a forcing vector.

In this lesson, we'll derive the formula for the particular solution of the above system using the method of variation of parameters.

Recall that the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_c(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{c}$ is a vector of constants, and $\Phi$ is the fundamental matrix.

As usual, for the method of variation of parameters, we'll look for a particular solution of our inhomogeneous system by varying the constant parameters, i.e., in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined.

Differentiating $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{'}(t) & =(Φ\,u(t))^{'} \\  & =Φ{u}^{'}(t)+{Φ}^{'}u(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a solution, substituting it back into the initial system gives a true equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{'}(t)+{Φ}^{'}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, $\Phi' = A \Phi.$ Substituting this into the equation simplifies it to the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{'}(t)+AΦu(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{'}(t) & =f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $\Phi$ is invertible, we can pre-multiply both sides by $\Phi^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{'}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{'}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate both sides of the final equations (ignoring the constant term):

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{'}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \displaystyle\int \Phi^{-1}\mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "99630576-f78f-593a-af83-87c98421e2c0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14396 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "94760db8-7585-5363-8838-c0f44735b806" :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166985} {:db/id 17592186167896 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167991 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of ordinary differential equations

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) =
A
\mathbf{x}(t) +
\mathbf{f}(t)
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix and $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is a forcing vector.

In this lesson, we'll derive the formula for the particular solution of the above system using the method of variation of parameters.

Recall that the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_c(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{c}$ is a vector of constants, and $\Phi$ is the fundamental matrix.

As usual, for the method of variation of parameters, we'll look for a particular solution of our inhomogeneous system by varying the constant parameters, i.e., in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined.

Differentiating $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{'}(t) & =(Φ\,u(t))^{'} \\  & =Φ{u}^{'}(t)+{Φ}^{'}u(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a solution, substituting it back into the initial system gives a true equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{'}(t)+{Φ}^{'}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, $\Phi' = A \Phi.$ Substituting this into the equation simplifies it to the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{'}(t)+AΦu(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{'}(t) & =f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $\Phi$ is invertible, we can pre-multiply both sides by $\Phi^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{'}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{'}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate both sides of the final equations (ignoring the constant term):

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{'}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \displaystyle\int \Phi^{-1}\mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "99630576-f78f-593a-af83-87c98421e2c0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14396 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "94760db8-7585-5363-8838-c0f44735b806" :step/math-academy-id 592305 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167897}} {:db/id 17592186167991 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of ordinary differential equations

:question/worked-solution "We must factor the quadratic expression
$10a^2 + 11a + 3$.

First, we find two numbers that

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($10 \times 3 = 30$), and
- add to the linear coefficient ($11$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $30$.

The positive factor pairs of $30$ are
$(1,30), \quad (2,15), \quad (3,10), \quad (5,6)$.

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(5,6)$ add to $11{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
5 + 6 &= 11✓
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $5a + 6a$, and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}
10a^{2} + 11a + 3 &=  \\
10a^{2} + 5a + 6a + 3 &=  \\
(10a^{2} + 5a) + (6a + 3) &=  \\
5a(2a + 1) + 3(2a + 1) &=  \\
&= (5a + 3)(2a + 1)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049074} {:db/id 17592186064476 :question/id #uuid "acf95ff0-c23c-5538-9064-3e039f763a54" :question/math-academy-id "q-111835" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064247 expression $2c^2 + 15c - 8$." :question/worked-solution "We must factor the quadratic expression
$2c^2 + 15c - 8$.

First, we find two numbers that

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($2 \times -8 = -16$), and
- add to the linear coefficient ($15$).

First, we find the factor pairs of $-16{:}$
$(1,-16),\quad (-1,16), \quad (2,-8), \quad (-2,8), \quad (4,-4)$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-1,16)$ add to $15{:}$

$$
(-1) + 16 = 15 \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

Then, rewrite the linear term as $-c+16c$, and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2c^{2} + 15c - 8 &=  \\
2c^{2} - c + 16c - 8 &=  \\
(2c^{2} - c) + (16c - 8) &=  \\
c(2c - 1) + 8(2c - 1) &=  \\
&= (2c - 1)(c + 8)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064617 :question/id #uuid "95f89ff5-94d5-5b32-a6fa-bcc8e91137d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-224927"} {:db/id 17592186064695 :question/id #uuid "dc06db78-79be-54a6-bd31-b5d3fec1e32f" :question/math-academy-id "q-2845"} {:db/id 17592186064751 :question/id #uuid "d5a223d5-f990-5f7c-8bf1-cb8f620bff13" :question/math-academy-id "q-33887"} {:db/id 17592186064249 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064003 :question/id #uuid "ad032833-ecf8-5295-9a9f-f69f759c19b0" :question/math-academy-id "e-15072"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0d5115f8-05b7-5df5-92b1-b4faa95f8449" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064614 :question/id #uuid "fc431e2b-deaa-50ac-bb6c-e24b275b504c" :question/math-academy-id "q-224888"} {:db/id 17592186064615 :question/id #uuid "a3e831d3-abc2-55e9-bf9b-dc61742297fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-224896"} {:db/id 17592186064616 :question/id #uuid "32c14ac4-d421-5d0c-b8af-4d8855fd2e30" :question/math-academy-id "q-224920"}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Coefficients and Positive Constants"} {:db/id 17592186064003 :question/id #uuid "ad032833-ecf8-5295-9a9f-f69f759c19b0" :question/math-academy-id "e-15072" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186064249 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0d5115f8-05b7-5df5-92b1-b4faa95f8449" :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Coefficients and Positive Constants"}] :question/problem "Factor the expression $3x^2 - 16x + 16$." :question/worked-solution "We must factor the quadratic expression

First, we find two numbers that

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($3 \times 16 = 48$), and
- add to the linear coefficient ($-16$).

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the product of the quadratic coefficient and constant is positive, we only need to consider the negative factor pairs of $48$.

The negative factor pairs of $48$ are
$(-1,-48), \quad (-2,-24), \quad (-3,-16), \quad (-4,-12), \quad (-6,-8)$.

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-4,-12)$ add to $-16{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
(-4) + (-12) &= -16✓
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-4x - 12x$, and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x^{2} - 16x + 16 &=  \\
3x^{2} - 4x - 12x + 16 &=  \\
(3x^{2} - 4x) - (12x - 16) &=  \\
x(3x - 4) - 4(3x - 4) &=  \\
&= (x - 4)(3x - 4)
\end{aligned}

one. In this lesson, we'll extend our understanding to include cases where the quadratic coefficient is a positive integer that's different from one.

For example, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
{\color{red}{2}}x^2+{\color{purple}{7}}x+{\color{blue}{3}}
$$

Notice that the quadratic coefficient equals ${\color{red}{2}}$.

To factor this trinomial, we must find two numbers that

- *multiply* to give the *product* of the quadratic coefficient and the constant $({\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{blue}{3}} = 6)$, and
- *add* to give the linear coefficient $({\color{purple}{7}})$.

We can factor this trinomial in four steps:

- **Step 1:** We start by writing down the factor pairs of $6{:}$The factor pairs of $6$ are
$(1,6), \qquad (2,3)$.

- **Step 2:** Determine which of these factor pairs add up to the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{7}})$:
$\begin{bmatrix}1 + 6|= 7 & ✓ \\ 2 + 3|= 5 & \cdot\end{bmatrix}$

- **Step 3:** Using the factor pair identified in the previous step, write the linear term as $7x=x+6x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x^{2} + 7x + 3 &=  \\
&= 2x^{2} + x + 6x + 3
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 4:** Factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:
$2x^{2} + x + 6x + 3|=; x(2x + 1) + 3(2x + 1)|=; (2x + 1)(x + 3)$.

And we're done!

We can check that our answer is correct by expanding the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2x + 1)(x + 3) &=  \\
2x \cdot (x + 3) + 1 \cdot (x + 3) &=  \\
2x^{2} + 6x + x + 3 &=  \\
2x^{2} + 7x + 3 &= ✓
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f7e6d3a2-936b-5775-9cf9-10135f0e6486" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9455 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c655bc80-5885-54d2-8a94-0ad9c1a41019" :step/math-academy-id 177992 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065120}} {:db/id 17592186065120 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064247 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064002 :question/id #uuid "44cf8c85-f228-5eaa-922d-613355cb7d5b" :question/math-academy-id "e-15070"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7f6a7917-f877-5263-abea-a78c0707d9fc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049074}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064476} {:db/id 17592186064577} {:db/id 17592186064613}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomial With Positive Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "462ef775-e55e-588f-acaf-4bf8f7bdc2df" :step/math-academy-id 177993 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065121}} {:db/id 17592186065121 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064248 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064004 :question/id #uuid "35bedd9f-bcb7-5024-bfe7-5ef6d34518bc" :question/math-academy-id "e-15073"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8cfe2121-66f0-53fa-b744-041fe830bf13" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064617} {:db/id 17592186064695} {:db/id 17592186064751}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Constants"} :step/id #uuid "1a35042e-19b9-53df-b251-f234f0733094" :step/math-academy-id 177997 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065122}} {:db/id 17592186065122 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065450 :tutorial/content "To factor a quadratic expression, we must find a factor pair of the *product* of the quadratic coefficient and the constant that adds to the linear coefficient.

With that in mind, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
{\color{red}{2}}y^2 {\color{purple}{\,-\,7}}y + {\color{blue}{3}}
$$

Notice that,

- the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant, ${\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{blue}{3}} = 6$, is *positive*, while
- the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}})$ is *negative*.

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the product of the quadratic coefficient and constant is positive, we need to consider the *negative* factor pairs of $6$.

The negative factor pairs of $6$ are
$(-1,-6), \quad (-2,-3)$.
For each pair, their *product* is positive, and their sum is *negative*, which is what we want.

Now, we determine which of these factor pairs sums to the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}}){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
(-1) + (-6) &= -7✓ \\
(-2) + (-3) &= -5\cdot
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-y - 6y$, and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2y^{2} - 7y + 3 &=  \\
2y^{2} - y - 6y + 3 &=  \\
(2y^{2} - y) - (6y - 3) &=  \\
y(2y - 1) - 3(2y - 1) &=  \\
&= (y - 3)(2y - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5ff88dae-40df-5a63-a7bd-0d73317e94a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9506 :tutorial/title "Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "412ba190-4d83-5be1-abb2-91fae26ca40e" :step/math-academy-id 178001 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065123}} {:db/id 17592186065123 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064249 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064003 :question/id #uuid "ad032833-ecf8-5295-9a9f-f69f759c19b0" :question/math-academy-id "e-15072"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0d5115f8-05b7-5df5-92b1-b4faa95f8449" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064614} {:db/id 17592186064615} {:db/id 17592186064616}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "e94449ef-31f1-5a5f-b3b9-9cc8fc6af17b" :step/math-academy-id 178002}] :activity/title "Factoring Trinomials With Leading Coefficients" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064458} {:db/id 17592186065119 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065449 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to factor quadratic trinomials whose quadratic coefficient equals one. $$
[\begin{aligned}a & 18 \\ 18 & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}c \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{2}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}16 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}24 & 18 \\ 18 & 17\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}18 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=24+17+18=59.

17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{2}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 4 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}12 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}14 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & ={[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}14 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12\cdot 5-(-6)\cdot (-6)}[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 6 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}14 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}40 \\ 24\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162351 :question/id #uuid "a22cb81e-00a5-5c3a-9983-3ce07b82cf44" :question/math-academy-id "q-137105" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8226456a-01f0-5577-ae2a-e36c51dc2d73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186159309} {:answer/id #uuid "97023f76-2165-5875-884b-00124cfc7eaf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186159310} {:answer/id #uuid "cd6021b0-6cc8-5e87-80d1-4225584902b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186159311} {:answer/id #uuid "32780e7c-aac0-5688-a09b-948445ba520b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186159312} {:answer/id #uuid "4b0c73b3-1f00-5eb0-b4a8-0954c2dec4c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186159313}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186159310} :answer-field/id #uuid "2914e011-6467-5eb9-b672-4230ceda87a3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186159308}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ shown above. If the general solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 16 & -8 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}72 & -36 \\ -36 & 18\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}20 \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}72 & -36 & 20 \\ -36 & 18 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}72 & -36 & 20 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{18}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{18}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{18} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
9a+\frac{b}{c}=9\cdot \frac{5}{18}+\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{1}=3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186269156 :question/id #uuid "670f8829-0bde-5ea3-bf13-816d75c51f2a" :question/math-academy-id "q-137917"} {:db/id 17592186269157 :question/id #uuid "80a60424-3ff9-5896-996b-077192e08a91" :question/math-academy-id "q-137920"} {:db/id 17592186269158 :question/id #uuid "f530dfca-e960-58b4-85b6-e3859f215c3f" :question/math-academy-id "q-137926" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162093 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b21c27bd-5c7a-5645-93b5-0af73c59f685" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Solution to a Weighted Least-Squares Problem"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "78477676-aaff-5c06-b1ee-eed5c9f6e6a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186267201} {:answer/id #uuid "790ad49f-51e6-5334-ae95-279f0ce3dc86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186267211} {:answer/id #uuid "bd677b76-300d-5ff0-a2d1-18c188c2bcc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186267841} {:answer/id #uuid "e775e691-a907-5ec0-a57d-a631428e4806" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186268196} {:answer/id #uuid "f4b80e3d-d6ae-5ee2-a000-d151a92c4224" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186268316}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "bd677b76-300d-5ff0-a2d1-18c188c2bcc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186267841} :answer-field/id #uuid "b8b344ad-6420-5f55-82f7-f81014532210" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186268734}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$

3135} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163036 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163308 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the least-squares problem $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where 

![](images/4d/4d538e6a37eccc1f49f34d3aa1b31a0539d50b351e6029595af1b1f7e0f2967a.svg)

Recall that the corresponding least-squares solution is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that 

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert
$$

is as small as possible.

In real-world problems, the coefficients stored in $A$ might come from sources that are not equally reliable. For example, the coefficients might be collected from population surveys with different sample sizes. As a result, we might want to assign a greater "weight" to the more reliable data.

For example, suppose we require the weight of the coefficients in the first row to be twice the weights of the other rows. Then, we can re-state our problem by saying that, for the matrix of weights $W,$ given by

![](images/72/7268fdd7c8701a9cf780342d6eab11015d7764694d17c28a2fae2336db267223.svg)

we wish to find vectors ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that 

$$
\Vert  W (A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}) \Vert
$$

is as small as possible.

Therefore, instead of solving $A\mathbf x = \mathbf{b},$ we now need to solve the least-squares problem 

$$
W\!A\mathbf x = W\mathbf{b}.
$$

To get the normal equation corresponding to this least-squares problem, we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\!A)^T{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

![](images/0c/0c7459270d9d27c40bdf5b0e6dc7eb0c7e17951541b77936804a9057f488c13f.svg)

the normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}36 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}72 \\ -54\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

"7800afe1-dfc0-5278-8b64-b02ebb92f823" :step/math-academy-id 36975 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163045}} {:db/id 17592186163045 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163312 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $A\mathbf x=\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ Furthermore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ that's closest to $\mathbf b.$ 

In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ Therefore, the error vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A).$

![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)

A similar property holds for weighted least-squares solutions:

*If the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $W\!A\mathbf x=W\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then
$A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i,
$$

 
where the $w_i$'s are the weights from the main diagonal of the weight matrix $W.$* 

We previously considered the weighted least-squares problem $W\!Ax=W\mathbf{b},$ where

![](images/d4/d44c48deb0864fb8fd6aa92ce8af408b600de8abf2039a3f3cd7397fabc7d9fe.svg)

It's easy to show (using the usual techniques) that the unique weighted least-squares solution is given by 

![](images/db/db8f62fcb085d8c1fcfc22bb53cb8f22bd9a65b211e5fd5d4017e30bf9bdb4c7.svg)

Computing our error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}ε & =A\overset{^}{x}-b \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 4 \\ 14\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $\mathbf a_1$ and $\mathbf a_2$ denote the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$ 
![](images/3f/3fbafcf3f9d80d2d54089647b2f0239662dcbe56c9ba68539e2303ce752d28ee.svg)

Notice that the error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is *not* orthogonal to the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{1} & =⟨[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]⟩ \\  & =(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =-3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{2} & =⟨[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]⟩ \\  & =(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we check the orthogonality with respect to the *weighted* dot product 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i = 4x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + x_3y_3,
\quad
$$

 

we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{⟨ε,{a}_{1}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =0\,✓ \\ {⟨ε,{a}_{2}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product. We can write this as

$$
A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \perp_W \textrm{Col}(A).
$$

{:db/id 17592186163045 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163312 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $A\mathbf x=\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ Furthermore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ that's closest to $\mathbf b.$ 

In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ Therefore, the error vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A).$

![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)

A similar property holds for weighted least-squares solutions:

*If the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $W\!A\mathbf x=W\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then
$A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i,
$$

 
where the $w_i$'s are the weights from the main diagonal of the weight matrix $W.$* 

We previously considered the weighted least-squares problem $W\!Ax=W\mathbf{b},$ where

![](images/d4/d44c48deb0864fb8fd6aa92ce8af408b600de8abf2039a3f3cd7397fabc7d9fe.svg)

It's easy to show (using the usual techniques) that the unique weighted least-squares solution is given by 

![](images/db/db8f62fcb085d8c1fcfc22bb53cb8f22bd9a65b211e5fd5d4017e30bf9bdb4c7.svg)

Computing our error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}ε & =A\overset{^}{x}-b \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 4 \\ 14\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $\mathbf a_1$ and $\mathbf a_2$ denote the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$ 
![](images/3f/3fbafcf3f9d80d2d54089647b2f0239662dcbe56c9ba68539e2303ce752d28ee.svg)

Notice that the error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is *not* orthogonal to the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{1} & =⟨[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]⟩ \\  & =(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =-3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{2} & =⟨[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]⟩ \\  & =(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we check the orthogonality with respect to the *weighted* dot product 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i = 4x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + x_3y_3,
\quad
$$

 

we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{⟨ε,{a}_{1}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =0\,✓ \\ {⟨ε,{a}_{2}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product. We can write this as

$$
A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \perp_W \textrm{Col}(A).
$$

In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection with respect to $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W$ of the vector $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ 

Furthermore, the weighted least-squares problem with weight matrix $W$ is equivalent to finding a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert_W
$$

is as small as possible." :tutorial/id #uuid "91e0f414-7785-5748-bba9-04278c6519ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6084 :tutorial/title "A Geometric Interpretation of the Weighted Least-Squares Solution"} :step/id #uuid "373b333f-64bb-5518-823a-a53a7c7b2614" :step/math-academy-id 37006} {:db/id 17592186163312 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $A\mathbf x=\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ Furthermore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ that's closest to $\mathbf b.$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$

$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{2}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 4 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}12 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}14 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -8 & 16 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -12 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}18 & -36 \\ -36 & 72\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}27 \\ -54\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}18 & -36 & 27 \\ -36 & 72 & -54\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}18 & -36 & 27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{3}{2}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$
a+\frac{b}{c}=2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+\frac{2}{1}=5.

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "47be74ee-5888-5dc1-a458-d8d8cd278e9e" :question/math-academy-id "q-137878" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ above. If the normal equation for the corresponding weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a & 20 \\ 20 & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}c \\ 29\end{aligned}]
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {3}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ -18 & -9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -27\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}37 & 20 \\ 20 & 17\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}55 \\ 29\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=37+17+55=109.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d09a6f63-a2b3-5d2d-bc98-fffbf81bdb65" :step/next {:db/id 17592186443609}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bf25468f-d230-53f1-a94f-8f18037a8dfd" :answer/type {:db/id $$
p_1(t)=3+2t, \qquad
	p_2(t)=-t+t^2.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $\mathcal{B}=\big\{ p_1(t), p_2(t) \big\}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1, p_2 \big\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ are ![](images/32/3274a690fa59f7d7368fcbe54004eab244c9845e20bf03ffce1e9fa25bbaf4bc.png)" :question/worked-solution "Any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1, p_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

![](images/17/170acd827e8b97471869159c5d9af88b0e4324b25ca1b42ec652011ece6a5174.png)

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =4\cdot (3+2t)+(-3)\cdot (-t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =12+8t+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =12+11t-3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048552} {:db/id 17592186167306 :question/id #uuid "f12f66c1-245b-53df-bb76-ad20f17b9b10" :question/math-academy-id "q-36474"} {:db/id 17592186167307 :question/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
{A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix $C$ given that $B={{A}_{1},{A}_{2}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}},$ and the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $B$ are $[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Any vector in $\text{Span}{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{A}_{1}+{x}_{2}{A}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=4 \\ 7{x}_{2}=14 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2\cdot 2 & =4 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =8 \\ {x}_{1} & =4.\end{aligned}

If $B={{B}_{1},{B}_{2}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that

$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$

$$

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{4}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & -2 \\ 0 & \frac{9}{2} & \frac{9}{2} \\ 0 & -\frac{5}{2} & -\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=-2 \\ \frac{9}{2}{x}_{2}=\frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{5}{2}{x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=1.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+6\cdot 1 & =-2 \\ 4{x}_{1} & =-8 \\ {x}_{1} & =-2.\end{aligned}

$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the following polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)={t}^{2}+t,\,{p}_{2}(t)={t}^{2}-2t+4,\,{p}_{3}(t)={t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}-2,\,\,q(t)=2+{t}^{2}+{t}^{3}.
$$

If $B={{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)},$ and $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)+{x}_{3}{p}_{3}(t)=q(t).
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}({t}^{2}+t)+{x}_{2}({t}^{2}-2t+4)+{x}_{3}({t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}-2) & =2+{t}^{2}+{t}^{3} \\ (4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3})+({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})t+({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}){t}^{2}+{x}_{3}{t}^{3} & =2+{t}^{2}+{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain 

$$
{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=1 \\ {x}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+2{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=1.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
4{x}_{2}-2\cdot 1=2\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=1.
$$

Now, substituting the obtained value into the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}-2\cdot 1=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and therefore ${x}_{1}=2.$"} {:db/id 17592186360540 :question/id #uuid "fd8162f1-9125-55c3-8d42-af30755391ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-95023" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166753 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2d8f8be0-0fe9-5734-87d3-5c432b7f298f" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Polynomial Vector Space"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b3aabddb-8f21-5ac4-85e0-911c0c8d8f98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186359318} {:answer/id #uuid "baaa715b-7689-55ee-b14e-fd88568d265c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186359375} {:answer/id #uuid "c6ea90f6-c8b2-51ad-92af-372a97869184" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186359502} {:answer/id #uuid "e785973e-4713-55d7-92da-c991e0d3c75b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186359803} {:answer/id #uuid "e864d953-5e40-5d07-977c-588765dcc861" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186359812}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "baaa715b-7689-55ee-b14e-fd88568d265c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186359375} :answer-field/id #uuid "b85ad7f6-b08d-59fb-bd7f-700836251219" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186360318}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2+t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=1-{t}^{2},\,q(t)=2+3t+4{t}^{2}.
$$

If $B={{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)},$ and $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=q(t)
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(2+t)+{x}_{2}(1-{t}^{2}) & =2+3t+4{t}^{2} \\ (2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+{x}_{1}t-{x}_{2}{t}^{2} & =2+3t+4{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2 \\ {x}_{1}=3 \\ -{x}_{2}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-4.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}+(-4)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=3+(-4)=-1.$"} {:db/id 17592186360542 :question/id #uuid "d482ef0a-c05c-5115-aa27-a3051b991631" :question/math-academy-id "q-95030"} {:db/id 17592186360543 :question/id #uuid $$

$$

$\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^n.$ In this lesson, we will generalize this concept to abstract vector spaces.

As an example, consider the matrices $A_1$ and $A_2,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

The set $\mathcal{B}=\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ is a basis of the vector space $V = \textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}.$ Now, suppose that the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ are 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Let's find the matrix $C$ using this information. 

As usual, any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
x_1 A_1  + x_2 A_2,
$$

where $x_1,x_2$ are the coordinates of the vector relative to the basis. 

In our case, we have 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]+4\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 12 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 10 \\ 8 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6638787f-3ef3-5623-bcec-de4b89ebfd02" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4962 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e61da532-1350-59ec-be76-0a0464423ad6" :step/math-academy-id :step/math-academy-id 30917 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167584}} {:db/id 17592186167584 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168065 :tutorial/content "Suppose we fix a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with scalars from $\mathbb{R}$ (note that "finite-dimensional" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element $\mathbf{v} \in V$ using the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]
$$

This defines a bijective mapping $\phi: V\to \mathbb{R}^n.$ Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:

- $\phi(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = \phi(\mathbf{u}) + \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V,$ and

- $\phi(\alpha \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}.$

Because of this, we say that $V$ is **isomorphic** to $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Intuitively, this means that $V$ and $\mathbb R^n$ have identical structures.

So, any finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some particular $n.$ This means that instead of studying all possible vector spaces, we can simply study only one family of vector spaces, namely $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n\geq 1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e501b24f-7ea0-5110-a4c5-e8739ea9ac11" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4964 :tutorial/title "Isomorphisms of Vector Spaces"} :step/id #uuid "f13dd7dd-f256-5871-9c5b-37fcd35b85a3" :step/math-academy-id 30920}] :activity/title "The Coordinates of a Vector Relative to a Basis in Abstract Vector Spaces" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166996} {:db/id 17592186167580 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168064 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to write the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf v\in \mathbb R^n$ relative some general basis $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^n.$ In this lesson, we will generalize this concept to abstract vector spaces.

{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),$ which is $5,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{2}{5}\cdot {5}^{2}=10\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186231570 :question/id #uuid "968f331f-040e-5a16-a459-23a91c08dfd4" :question/math-academy-id "q-343473" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231428 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2454e747-bfcd-5336-8dee-2dbbf5a40c37" :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Spring Constant Given an External Periodic Force"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "498bed50-28c7-50fa-a5df-0080495261c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186441791}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "498bed50-28c7-50fa-a5df-0080495261c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186441791} :answer-field/id #uuid "5abd7c36-14a4-56ef-ada9-6c206b80a9d0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186230295}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "A particle of mass $0.5\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. $f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)+3t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $1.$ Therefore,
$\omega =1.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =1$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(2D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡t-(2C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]+t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2D\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2C\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

Only solution I matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186231576 :question/id #uuid "a2dc0571-7d63-58c4-a7e9-b264e1dac3a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-343760" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231429 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cac41120-247d-5821-b7f6-b342dbcf8f18" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8588f05c-f259-5f6f-95a4-ba743efb8633" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None" :db/id 17592186230323} {:answer/id #uuid "87e2a5ac-5e6b-5176-ada3-76165f3827b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186230324} {:answer/id #uuid "bd0f684b-31be-53dd-959a-4c693200fbd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186230325} {:answer/id #uuid "ebbe1595-b0a0-5005-89d3-b1a66671386d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186230326} {:answer/id #uuid "6ad71e63-ab40-5319-b40d-20fec2c9d4de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186230327}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ebbe1595-b0a0-5005-89d3-b1a66671386d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186230326} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6c1fc5b-ecb6-509b-ab8e-ba64d464ed59" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186230322}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The external force is $f(t)=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(6D-9Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-(6C+9Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 6D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-6C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=\frac{1}{2}$ and $D=-2.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above.
